If a data center was coming, the commissioners felt that the developers should pay for the cost of the additional services it would require, an amount the county estimated to be $16.2 million. The county, Morris, and the developers haggled over the terms as the April 15th target passed and moved to April 22nd, the commission’s next scheduled meeting.
A public notice was issued for the vote. It appeared on the county’s upcoming agenda as item 9A, “Interlocal Agreement #26-15 Between Box Elder County and the Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA) Relating to the Stratos Project Area,” using a project name Morris said MIDA liked because it was Greek for “army.” There was no mention of a data center.
Anticipating blowback, Perry texted Pritchett to make sure that the landowners would show up to publicly say they were in favor of the project.
But with the contract still in flux, the commissioners postponed voting to a later meeting — “If you would like to speak to that, please fill a form out,” Vincent said — and the meeting instead became Stratos’ quiet debut. It was a small, subdued event. Shane Holmgren, the largest landowner and the first approached by Pritchett, was “100 percent supportive of this.” Others were less enthusiastic, worrying about traffic or water use. When Vincent asked for a show of hands for who was in favor of the project, someone shouted out, “What about those of us in the impact area who are undecided because we need more information?”
“The only one that enjoys change is a baby,” Tim Munns said, philosophically, at the meeting. After days of thinking and discussions with his family, he had decided to sell. It had been the military connection that convinced him. That and the project’s inevitability, he said.
“If it’s going to happen and we’re going to watch it happen in this valley, then we’re going to be at the table instead of being on the menu,” he later tells me.
Two days later, on Friday morning, MIDA held its own meeting to approve the project area. The paperwork wasn’t quite finished, Morris said, but it was 95 or 98 percent of the way there. Nor had the county itself given its consent. Morris said the commissioners would meet at 5 that afternoon — “the fastest they could put it together” — though the commissioners would again delay.
MIDA’s event was a more celebratory affair, consisting mostly of Morris and other MIDA officials marveling at the speed at which they had moved. O’Leary appeared on a video call, taking a seat before a photo of skyscrapers.
“Forty thousand acres, I don’t think there’s a bigger facility in the world than this.”
“What’s extraordinary about Utah is I heard about this opportunity just five months ago. That’s it. And here we are on the cusp of doing something absolutely phenomenal together. That’s leadership,” he said, thanking Cox, House Speaker Schultz, MIDA, and Adams, the Senate president who was also the chairman of the MIDA board. It was important to move fast, O’Leary said, because it was a race, not just with China, but with other data center projects, to win tenants. “But we have tenants knocking on our door,” O’Leary said. “My job is going to tell the world what we’ve done here.”
This was something O’Leary was well suited to do. He had spent two decades turning himself into one of the business world’s most visible promoters. O’Leary came up through educational software in the 1990s, acquiring rivals like The Learning Company, which he sold to Mattel in 1999 for roughly $4 billion. It was a disaster for Mattel, which was sued along with O’Leary for misrepresenting The Learning Company’s financial state. (Mattel settled.) Four years later, O’Leary cold-called an executive at a Canadian business channel with the pitch that he was good on TV, according to a 2012 profile by The Globe and Mail’s Report on Business. He got a role as a brash conservative news commentator, then as a judge on the CBC reality show Dragons’ Den, where he dispensed brutally frank appraisals of aspiring entrepreneurs’ business plans. He then reprised the role for the American version, Shark Tank. Last year, he played the villainous tycoon in Marty Supreme. An avatar of unapologetic wealth onscreen and off, he appeared on the Oscars red carpet wearing a $30 million basketball card encased in diamonds on a chain around his neck with matching Rolex and Cartier watches, one on each wrist.
He has parlayed his fame into several businesses, including O’Leary Ventures, O’Shares Investments, and O’Leary Fine Wines. In 2021, he took stakes in FTX in a deal to become a “spokesperson and ambassador” for the company, which collapsed the following year and whose CEO is currently in prison for fraud. His first foray into data centers came in 2022, when he invested in and promoted a bitcoin miner called Bitzero. (After posting net losses, the company recently repositioned itself as an AI compute provider.) In 2024, O’Leary announced a data center of his own, under his brand O’Leary Digital, in Greenview, Alberta. It would be enormous, according to the announcement: 7,000 acres, powered by a 7.5GW gas plant, later upgraded to 9GW.
“Introducing Wonder Valley: The Largest AI Compute Data Center Park on Earth,” he posted on X at the time, embedding a video of an eagle flying through renderings of a lush and futuristic campus.
“Wonder Valley Utah” would apparently also be the world’s largest. “Forty thousand acres, I don’t think there’s a bigger facility in the world than this,” O’Leary said on Fox and Friends three days after the MIDA vote. “We’re going to build the largest data center in the world here,” he said hours later in another Fox appearance. Then he posted the clip to his 4 million LinkedIn followers under a red banner that read, “WE’RE BUILDING THE WORLD’S LARGEST DATA CENTER IN UTAH.”
O’Leary’s hyperbole can be best understood as a pitch to the hyperscale tech companies about what the data center could be if they were to sign on as tenants, the investor Paul Kedrosky says. These investors don’t care whether AI turns out to be profitable. What they care about is that a very profitable tech company is going to occupy the data center and be contractually obligated to pay them a fixed return no matter how AI turns out. “It could be hide-and-seek competitions going on inside of these things,” Kedrosky says. “What they care about is how pristine the credit is of the hyperscalers involved.”
Mixed in with real construction projects are lots of paper data centers, speculative ventures announced as if they were shovel-ready
For developers, this presents what Palandjian, the CEO of O’Leary Digital, calls a “chicken-and-egg problem.” In order to finance construction of a data center, you need an anchor tenant, but all tenants care about is speed, so the best way to attract one is to get everything aside from the actual data center — land, power, permitting — ready to go. “If you’re talking to a hyperscaler today, they’ll say, ‘Don’t even talk to me unless you can show me a pathway to potentially lighting up my first data centers by mid 2028,’” Palandjian says.
This dynamic is part of the reason there are so many “world’s largest data centers,” more even than O’Leary’s two. Mixed in with real construction projects are paper data centers, speculative ventures specced out to their maximum theoretical capacity and announced as if they were shovel-ready with the aim of catching the attention of a hyperscale tenant. Many amount to nothing or very little. It’s been nearly two years since O’Leary announced his first Wonder Valley, in Alberta. There is still no publicly announced tenant, and according to the Greenview planning department, no permit applications have been filed.
The result is a structural dissonance in the data center buildout, where projects are pitched to a small group of tech titans in grandiose terms that to people who live near these projects sound maximally nightmarish. O’Leary brought a showman’s flair to the job.
“Kevin O’Leary isn’t pitching Utahns when he says, ‘We have 40,000 acres. It’s going to be the biggest data center ever,’” said Clint Betts, CEO of the Utah tech industry group Silicon Slopes. “He’s not even thinking about Utahns. He’s pitching potential tenants. And I think that’s what pisses Utahns off.”
Whether O’Leary’s pitch reached its intended audience was unclear. It unquestionably reached Utahns.
Brenna Williams heard about the data center at the grocery store. “You couldn’t walk down the hall someplace or go to McDonald’s or go out for coffee. Everybody was talking about it, and nobody was happy.”
Williams was particularly unhappy. In November, Joule Capital Partners had broken ground on a 4,000-acre data center campus 9 miles from her second home in western Utah, where she had planned to retire. A month later, work began nearby on another data center, this one 10GW and advertised as the world’s largest. Now there was a third data center, this one near her actual home in Box Elder, where she had raised two kids stargazing and rock hunting in the desert, also calling itself the world’s largest.
“We have to report on our neighbors if they’re watering at the wrong times or on the wrong days. But we have water to cool a power plant?”
Williams, a former government econometrician and college instructor, speaks methodically in a calm monotone as she enumerates the many reasons why the data center “doesn’t make sense” — a refrain. First among them is the water, an acutely sensitive issue in Utah in part thanks to Gov. Cox himself, who has declared repeated drought emergencies and urged residents to take shorter showers and cut back on watering their lawns. There is no more potent symbol of the state’s water crisis than the Great Salt Lake, which has been shrinking for years, exposing heavy metals on its lakebed that become airborne dust. Now here came a data center on its northern shore, or where its northern shore would have been if it hadn’t receded several miles.
“We have to report on our neighbors if they’re watering at the wrong times or on the wrong days,” Williams says. (There’s a hotline.) “But we have water to cool a power plant and cool the data center? It doesn’t make sense.”
The question of data center water use is best thought of as a tradeoff between water and energy. Servers produce heat, and that heat must be removed from the building. An energy-efficient way of doing so is to transfer the heat into water, some of which evaporates, but the amount of water lost to evaporation can be significant. Google’s data center in The Dalles, Oregon, is cooled in this manner. A much smaller facility than the gigawatt-scale projects being proposed today, it consumed about 469 million gallons of water in 2025, about as much as 17 golf courses.
“We’ve been told that that needs to happen this month, whether that’s true or not.”
Heat can also be ejected directly into the outside air, similar to a home air conditioner’s exhaust. This method can use very little water, but it uses more of the electricity data centers already consume in immense quantities — electricity that, depending on how it’s generated, also uses water. According to a 2024 analysis from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, such “indirect” water consumption is about 12 times greater than the amount of water data centers consume on-site. For data centers like Stratos that intend to generate power on-site, this water use — and other externalities that once happened somewhere else on the grid — becomes direct and acute.
As is currently common in the industry, the Stratos developers and MIDA officials emphasized that the data center itself would use a “closed-loop cooling system” that would be filled once and reused. The county’s agreement with MIDA even specifically forbids water-intensive evaporative cooling. But the agreement also stipulates that none of these protections apply to the power plant, and it is the power plant that is listed as the primary use in the project’s applications for water rights.
Williams did not typically attend commission meetings, but when one was scheduled for the Monday after the MIDA vote, she showed up early and took a seat inside the courthouse, intending to make her displeasure known. So did around a hundred other people, more than the room could fit. They stood in the back, some holding signs, filled the hallway outside, spilled out onto the front steps.
They would not, however, get the opportunity to speak. “Public comment was held last week,” Vincent replied to a shouted question, though at that first meeting, where attendees primarily consisted of landowners the developer had personally invited, Vincent had promised a second comment period at the next meeting.
“I didn’t hear anything about it!” someone shouted.
“It was noticed,” said Vincent, banging his gavel.
“Very quietly!”
Vincent threatened to remove hecklers.
The commissioners went on to question Pritchett and a MIDA official named Hilary Venable for an hour with vague results. No one could explain what percentage of the facility was for military use or even what that use would be.
Regarding the water use of the gas plant, Pritchett said they would use “new air-cooling technologies that are zero water,” or at least he was pretty sure they would — the “exact technology partnerships of the newer power technology are not totally solidified.” (“I’m hearing a lot of ‘if’s,’” someone shouted from the audience.) When Perry asked why the commission was being rushed, Pritchett replied that actually, he was being rushed too. That zero-water turbine was slated to go to another state, Morris previously said, but Utah had the chance to snag it if they moved fast. “We’ve been told that that needs to happen this month, whether that’s true or not,” Pritchett said. “That’s the reason for the rush.”
Perry’s announcement that the commissioners would postpone their vote for another week to sort through all the questions they’d received from constituents was met with cheers from the audience. Next time, Perry said, the meeting would be held at the county fairground to accommodate the apparently large public interest.
According to an August survey from Heatmap, 75 percent of Americans would oppose a data center being built near them. People feel more positively about nuclear power plants by a 20-point margin. Dislike of data centers might be the most unifying issue in America today, though it is less that everyone is in agreement, one Utah activist told me, than that data centers provide something for everyone to hate.
Some oppose data centers on environmental grounds. Others find them ugly. They are such large industrial projects that solving one problem tends to raise others: Avoid raising electricity prices by building a power plant and air pollution and noise become problems. When Pritchett tried to assuage water concerns by promising an air-cooled gas turbine, a physics professor at Utah State University, Robert Davies, did some back-of-the-envelope math and estimated that Stratos would emit enough heat to raise nighttime temperatures by up to 12 degrees, above the dewpoint, potentially creating a Sahara-like climate in the valley.
That these enormous projects often arrive with little warning only intensifies the opposition, especially because their approval generally runs through local government. Americans may distrust Congress, corporations, and the media, but a majority does still trust their local government. It’s where people still expect democracy to work. The ability of small groups of citizens to block development is so great that some see it as a national crisis; in a county like Box Elder, residents can complain to their commissioners about fairground price hikes and elicit actual policy changes.
There was a different set of rules for the O’Learys and Zuckerbergs of the world
That trust helps explain the extraordinary emotion on display at data center meetings: Across the country, residents scream at their commissioners, sometimes break down in tears, after learning that their representatives approved a project they barely knew existed. The outrage is a level above disagreement with a land use decision. It feels like betrayal.
In Utah, the speed at which Stratos seemed to materialize was taken by some as evidence of conspiracy. Unsubstantiated claims of bribery were leveled at everyone from Cox, whose family founded the telecom company CentraCom, to the commissioners, because they might get seats on a MIDA advisory board. Dozens of people submitted comments to the county’s website alleging corruption and “back-room deals.” How else could something so big come together so fast?
Few believed the developers’ claims about water use and few trusted government assurances that Stratos would need to follow state environmental regulations no matter what technology it ended up using. Loopholes would be found, promises broken. There seemed to be a different set of rules for the O’Learys and Zuckerbergs of the world; just look at the speed at which this moved, one resident said, compared to the meetings and permitting he’d have to go through in order to install a swimming pool.
Strange political alignments began to form. Progressive activists like Deeda Seed, senior campaigner at the environmental group Center for Biological Diversity, found herself on the same side as Phil Lyman, a far-right former state representative who in 2020 was pardoned by Donald Trump for a conviction resulting from leading an ATV ride through a canyon closed to protect Native American cliff dwellings. Seed worried about the environmental impacts. Lyman hated the tax incentives and back-room dealing. Both felt democracy had been flouted and the people cut out of the process, a sentiment that Cox doused with gasoline when he said that slowing development with lengthy processes was “the dumbest thing ever.”
“We think that taking time makes things better or safer. It absolutely does not,” Cox said.
Even law enforcement officials monitoring the growing backlash noticed that something unusual was happening. Ahead of the commission meeting, an intelligence analyst with the Utah Statewide Information and Analysis Center (SIAC) emailed a sheriff to say that while there were no concrete threats, people were “very angry,” and at least two of them had posted GIFs of guillotines. Notably, the groups attending the meeting were of “opposing ideologies” and typically only meet when counterprotesting each other. “However, in today’s circumstance, they will be in the same space for the same purpose.”
“You can vote no, and we’ll find another way to make it happen”
On the advice of the law enforcement, the commissioners parked on the side of the road several miles from the fairground and were taken by squad car to the metal hangar-like hall where the meeting would be held. They toured the space — a basketball court with its bleachers withdrawn and scoreboard dark, rows of folding chairs facing a table draped in American flag bunting — and went to a back room to wait and go over their notes as they listened to the crowd gather outside.
Over the preceding days, the commissioners had been inundated with thousands of messages urging them to slow or stop the project. They had also received several calls from state lawmakers and officials telling them to vote yes.
“Would love to talk to you about the AI project if you have some time,” state Rep. Tom Peterson texted Perry on April 27th.
“Hey Lee, Scott here. Just wanted to, uh, pick your brain, compare a few notes, share a few thoughts on the data center when you get a minute, give me a call,” state Sen. Sandall said in a voicemail the next day.
Perry also got calls from the governor’s office and from the speaker of the house, he said. “They all kept saying, This is a great thing for the state of Utah. We need to get it done.”
As the date of the fairground meeting neared, MIDA became increasingly forceful, Perry and Vincent both said. MIDA had now given them one supposedly final deadline after another, and the commission had missed each one. Now a fourth vote was scheduled, and the public opposition was only growing.
“Please be quiet. Be courteous. Isn’t that who we are in the state of Utah?”
“That’s when they came in and told us, ‘Well, if you guys just really feel like you have to vote no, you can vote no, and we’ll find another way to make it happen,’” Perry said. “‘But just so you know, you won’t get any of the protections or any of the guardrails that you’ve negotiated, and you certainly won’t get the amount of tax money that we’ve been talking about.’”
Morris did not respond to requests for comment.
The lawyer the commission had retained agreed that the county had little power to stop the project, Perry and Vincent say. Still, Perry wrote two speeches the day before: one where he voted yes and another where he voted no, acknowledging the public outrage and warning that they may all have to pay higher taxes to fund the legal fight likely to come. Despite the furor, he did not have a clear sense that that was what his constituents wanted. Many of the messages he’d received came from nearby counties — Utahns who cared about the lake and air pollution but would not have to fund the county’s possible legal defense. Nor would they see their taxes drop once revenue from the data center started coming in. Perry would prefer to publicly discuss these pros and cons, but they had been too busy figuring out what the project even was and now there was no time. Ideally, he says, the state would have convened these town halls and also “come and told the public how we’re having this crammed down our throat.”
“For hell’s sake, grow up!”
When the commissioners finally walked out, they saw more than a thousand people filling the hall, many holding signs. They were greeted with applause as they took their seats. But the mood shifted the moment Vincent said, “Just a couple of housekeeping things: As last Monday, there will be no public comment period.”
The crowd erupted in boos.
“Enough, enough. Quiet down right now,” yelled Vincent, his voice going hoarse, banging the gavel. “Please be quiet. Be courteous. Isn’t that who we are in the state of Utah?”
Vincent proceeded to read from a prepared statement.
“It will generate jobs and economic investment in infrastructure—”
Booing.
“The closed-loop design means the data center won’t consume any more water than a typical office park or an— “
Booing.
Williams, in the audience, was frustrated both by what she was hearing and with the hecklers, because she wanted to hear what the commissioners had to say. Some in the audience called for quiet, but they were overpowered by the crowd, which roared at every mention of electricity, water, or possible benefits.
“Plus, it will create jobs, boost our local economy, and strengthen our military for years to come— “
Booing.
“We tried to get the department of Air Quality to come, but since no application has been filed, they would not. However, I was able to speak with an engineer—” the county attorney said, to more boos.
“Did you mention something about the dark sky thing?” Bingham tried to ask the county lawyer. “We had an agreement with MIDA on that.”
Yelling, booing, whistling.
“For hell’s sake, grow up!” Bingham shouted, eliciting more and louder boos.
A contingent began to chant: “People over profit!”
And with that, the commissioners stood, walked off the stage, and went into a back room, their contingency plan if the crowd became unruly. After 15 minutes of confused milling about, the crowd watched as a projection screen descended from the ceiling and the commissioners reappeared on video, now seated behind a folding table in a small fluorescent-lit room, police officers standing by the doorway. The meeting resumed and they voted to approve the project area. Behind the door, they could hear the crowd chant, “Shame, shame, shame.”
The sheriff told the commissioners to wait for the crowd to disperse before heading home. That evening, Sen. Sandall texted Perry, “You did the right thing.”
The image of elected officials fleeing their constituents to approve a data center in a literal back room was immediately explosive. Video of Bingham’s “For hell’s sake, grow up” was clipped, turned into songs, and seen by millions. O’Leary’s boasts about a 40,000-acre site was transformed through viral telephone into a data center that was itself three times the size of Manhattan, depicted with an image of a building footprint overlaying the city. Davies’ heat analysis headlined countless posts about the project releasing heat equivalent to 23 atomic bombs each day, the most alarming of several comparisons he made. There were many, many posts about billionaires and the Great Salt Lake and the biggest data center in the world, often illustrated with pictures of grinning O’Leary fanning himself with hundred-dollar bills. Data center outrage has become a social media staple, and it would be hard to design a more incendiary set of ingredients than Stratos.
“You could feel the heat coming off the keyboards, there was so much anger.”
All manner of online personalities converged on the story. There were environmental activists, travel influencers, guys in windowless rooms talking about the technocratic superstate, and hustlers shilling get-rich-with-AI courses trying to draft off the viral fury. The comedian Walter Masterson went to O’Leary’s neighborhood in Miami Beach with a petition to put the data center in his backyard. A prominent Utah drought-resistant gardener posted about boycotting the nursery of Sen. Jerry Stevenson, who sits on the MIDA board; when a reporter approached Stevenson in the parking lot, the senator called “the whole thing such a bunch of baloney” and slapped the phone out of his hand.
In Box Elder, Williams had gone home from the fairground vote furious and logged in to Facebook. So had dozens of other residents. “You could feel the heat coming off the keyboards, there was so much anger,” she said.
Brigette Cottam, a Brigham City mother of four, had missed the meeting but saw the video of Bingham shouting “for hell’s sake, grow up” — “Oh, they yelled at us?” — and also logged on. “Doomscrolling, I just saw post after post after post, like, what do we even do about this? What can we do about this?”
So she googled what to do when your county commissioners pass something nobody wants. The answer was to file a referendum, in this case one challenging the county’s consent to the project. Facebook pinged with volunteers. “Me, me, me, me. It was like ‘I am Spartacus,’” Cottam said.
The next morning, Williams, Cottam, and three others met at the Box Elder County Courthouse to get the paperwork. Later that week, they convened again, now with two dozen people around a nearby picnic table, and assigned roles. They called the group Box Elder Accountability Referendum, or BEAR, and started referring to themselves as “mama bears” in their posts. Soon they had 2,500 volunteers signed up.
Box Elder is a conservative county. Nearly 80 percent voted for Trump in the last election, including Williams. She describes the BEAR coalition as spanning “MAGA to Marxist.” Her husband is MAGA; her son, Marxist. They try not to discuss politics, except the data center, which unites them.
Utah’s Republican primary was just over a month away — often the decisive election in the deeply Republican state — and as outrage over the data center grew, politicians who had been instrumental in its arrival began distancing themselves from the project.
Cox said that he’d heard from Utahns with “real concerns” about environmental impact and tweeted that the developers had agreed to seek approval for the project in phases rather than all at once, something that almost certainly would have been the case anyway. “The process was not good,” Cox later said, adding that he had long been concerned about MIDA. “That was not a decision that was made by me or the legislature.”
“Hopefully some people will lose attention to the matter and others will see it as a win.”
House Speaker Schultz, who Perry said had called him before the vote to tell him the project was good for Utah and the county, now said he supported BEAR’s referendum.
The backtracking infuriated Adams, the Senate president and MIDA chair, who now found himself alone in an increasingly competitive primary challenge, according to a source with knowledge of his campaign.
With state officials running for cover, the Box Elder County commissioners were left defending their vote as the least bad option. The public’s fury did not abate. Police were stationed outside the commissioners’ homes. Someone emailed Perry telling him to light himself on fire. Perry choked up speaking about threats he’d received with news station KSL. Soon, they stopped giving interviews at all. Their campaign signs lining the streets of Brigham City were defaced with red spray paint reading “AI traitor.”
The developers too attempted an appeasement campaign. This wasn’t going to be the ugly concrete box you’re thinking of, Palandjian told the design publication Dezeen, unveiling renderings depicting a modernist glass building nestled beneath mountains glowing at golden hour. Yes, there might be a “man camp” housing the thousands of construction workers, but it was going to be the best man camp you’ve ever seen. “We want this to be the sexiest, coolest construction posting in America,” he said. “We want a beautiful, poetic design.”
The developer withdrew a water rights application that had garnered thousands of protests. It was a tactical move. Pritchett texted Perry that their plans remained unchanged. “Hopefully some people will lose attention to the matter and others will see it as a win,” Pritchett wrote.
They did not. In fact, the move only made people angrier, because filing a protest required paying a fee. Now 3,000 people felt O’Leary had personally stiffed each of them out of $15. A local professional skier and environmental activist posted a video of herself calling the Division of Water Resources and confirming that no, they would not be getting refunds.
“What the hell are they taking Chinese money for?”
In any case, all these conciliatory gestures were doomed to fail because at the same time, O’Leary was repeatedly going on television and posting about how his critics were bussed-in “professional protesters” working for the Chinese Communist Party.
“What the hell are they taking Chinese money for?” O’Leary exclaimed on May 20th, in one of several similar appearances on Fox during the period. “All proven all through these nefarious entities,” he said, holding up a colorful chart and claiming to have received a call from five government “special agents” interested in his investigation.
A few days later I called Palandjian, who went into more detail. “Everybody’s freaked out about AI and what it could do. AI is here already. We have the ability with our data scientists to see, you see those same five protesters that are in Utah protesting this project were in Michigan protesting that data center project. They’re on college campuses protesting and spouting antisemitic things. It’s all part of the same thing. And before that, BLM and antifa.”
When I asked whether he had performed facial recognition on the protesters, he said no, he meant that those tools existed, but “we’ve seen JPEGs.”
Maybe on a different issue O’Leary could have mustered some politically polarized support. With data centers, though, he encountered mostly skepticism, even from the right. When he went on Tucker Carlson’s show, Carlson, ever an astute reader of the national mood, dismissed O’Leary’s China fears. Instead, he repeatedly challenged him to explain why data centers were good for Americans rather than being an aesthetic “offense against God and nature” that raises their energy bills and takes their jobs.
As for Utahns themselves, having a Canadian celebrity tycoon accuse them of being bussed-in Chinese agents just made them even angrier.
By the time I arrived in Box Elder in mid-May, it seemed that O’Leary had succeeded in uniting the entire state both against his data center and himself personally. The activists he had called Chinese agents were doing a brisk business selling merch making fun of his “Utah National Security” hat. At a protest at the Capitol, there were as many signs attacking O’Leary as there were about data centers: “Keep sharks out of Great Salt Lake,” “Mr. Terrible,” and many jokes about being paid by China. At a gathering at the fairground, a resident prefaced his concerns with his Utah bona fides: third-generation Utahn, grew up duck hunting, and one of the lobbyists O’Leary hired, Casey Hill, “is literally my first cousin, so Casey, tell your boss Kevin that I didn’t get shipped in,” he said to laughter.
“What does it mean to beat China in the AI race? What does it mean to lose?”
They were against Stratos for all the reasons people are against data centers: concerns about water use, air pollution, noise, ugliness, tax breaks for wealthy corporations and billionaires. Yet many industrial projects share these problems and elicit nothing like the breadth and emotional intensity of the data center backlash. It’s popular to attribute the intensity to anxieties about AI itself, that data centers are only a physical proxy for people’s feelings about a threatening new technology. But in Box Elder, when AI was invoked at all, it was usually to illustrate the lack of any discernable reason for the project. A power plant would offer cheaper electricity. A factory might promise jobs making products people use. To many of the people I spoke with, the need for the data center was inexplicable, its benefits theoretical; the only thing clear about it was its cost.
“We don’t need this!” said Kristen Hadley at a commission meeting. She had not planned to speak but had become emotional listening to people list their fears to the impassive commissioners. She was 56 years old and had been told by her three daughters that the world was “too dangerous and toxic” to bring grandchildren into, she said, beginning to cry. She had watched the lake dry up. Now here came an enormous industrial project, and for what? “I didn’t need AI. AI was put on my phone without my knowledge.”
Few believed the public rationale for Stratos, that it was needed to beat China.
“What does it mean to beat China in the AI race? What does it mean to lose?” asked Betts, of Silicon Slopes. “I’ve been in tech my whole life, and I don’t know what it means, and I don’t think our leaders know what it means.”
People were so unconvinced by the given explanations for the AI buildout that some invented their own nefarious reasons that billionaires and government officials might have for urgently building gigantic data centers all over the country. Residents told commissioners that the data center was going to be used by the government to surveil opponents of Project 2025 and by the United Nations to carry out something called Agenda 21. The phrase “virtual prison” came up a lot.
It’s reassuring to imagine there is any such plan behind the data center frenzy rather than an arms race inside an arms race driven forward by financial speculation, a runaway process that even the people who initiated it hypothesize might end with the entire planet tiled with data centers. Facing the growing backlash, AI executives have lately tried to sketch a more enticing future, emphasizing the possibility of abundance and empowerment in addition to human extinction. Yet for people on the ground in Utah, it is hard to imagine they will share in this utopian future when the people building the data centers that enable it forgot to let them know it was coming and, when they raised objections, moved forward anyway. Whatever the true purpose of this civilization-scale mustering of industrial resources was, people sensed it was not for them, and they had no better evidence than the process itself.
Box Elder’s attorney rejected BEAR’s referendum; BEAR sued, and the case is ongoing. But the June primary brought a political reckoning.
In a last-minute gambit to get on the right side of the electorate, Adams sent a public letter to O’Leary demanding he scale down the project. O’Leary agreed to remove half of the allotted 40,000 acres, resulting in media coverage reporting that the project had been cut in half despite the fact that it was never clear what would go on that land and the scale of the data center itself remained unchanged. In any case, the gambit failed. Adams lost, becoming the most powerful political figure brought down by the data center backlash so far.
At MIDA, Morris, the executive director who’d spearheaded the project, retired. His replacement was Dan Hemmert, a former Utah senator and MIDA consultant who worked on Stratos. Cox says he will be pushing for “major reform” of the agency.
In Box Elder, Bingham and Perry both lost their primaries.
Perry still thinks approving the deal was the only real option, but he keeps running through other scenarios in his mind. Maybe if he’d called a press conference immediately after that first MIDA meeting, he wonders, he could have embarrassed the state into backing down. Maybe he could have made the MIDA officials hold town halls and face the public anger themselves. “But that’s all hindsight,” he says. His advice to other commissioners: Pass a moratorium on new data centers; if you have unzoned land, zone it. It will at least give you some time to figure out what your options are.
O’Leary continues to say that the project is “full steam ahead” and that he hopes to break ground in the next 12 months on the first phase, which has been downsized to a single gigawatt.
But little has happened since the county’s May 4th vote. Though MIDA had spent weeks warning commissioners that their consent could not wait, by late September the county remained the only party to have signed the interlocal agreement. Citing ongoing litigation over the referendum, MIDA has left its own signature blank and paused work on Stratos. The agency declined further comment, also citing the referendum and litigation. None of the land allotted for Stratos has been sold, and no tenant has been announced.
When the project resumes, it will face a less friendly political landscape. In August, Utah lawmakers inundated with constituent messages and unnerved by the fall of Adams held hearings on data center regulation in preparation for next year’s session. The commissioner of the Utah Department of Environmental Quality called noise and heat “major gaps” the agency planned to study.
The prospect of regulation and determined opposition may make occupancy less attractive. As will the project’s infamy. AI companies are coming to the belated realization that they have a public image problem, and true to his word, O’Leary did make sure the world heard about Stratos. There is likely no better-known data center on the planet.
articles.summary:
Celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary’s plan to build the world’s largest AI data center in rural Utah has stalled following intense public backlash and a series of political repercussions.

### Key Points
- The "Wonder Valley" project, later renamed Stratos, proposed a 40,000-acre data center campus in Box Elder County powered by a 9-gigawatt gas plant.
- Local residents and activists organized a massive opposition movement after learning the project was fast-tracked by state officials with minimal public input.
- O’Leary faced widespread criticism and a defamation lawsuit after baselessly accusing project opponents of being funded by the Chinese Communist Party.
- The political fallout led to the primary election defeats of several key supporters, including state Senate President J. Stuart Adams and two county commissioners.
- As of late August, the project remains stalled with no announced tenants, no land transfers, and ongoing legal challenges regarding a public referendum.

### Why it Matters
The controversy highlights the growing friction between the rapid, speculative expansion of AI infrastructure and the concerns of local communities regarding water usage, environmental impact, and transparency. This case serves as a cautionary tale for developers and policymakers, demonstrating that bypassing public engagement can trigger significant political instability and jeopardize multi-billion-dollar industrial projects.

articles.title: Exclusive: Neurable’s First Brain-Scanning Headphones Want to Fine-Tune Your Focus
articles.author: Julian Chokkattu
articles.content:
Neurable unveiled its very own pair of brain-scanning headphones on Thursday, the Neurable One. The company claims that wearing them helps you concentrate on whatever you’re doing—working, studying, or playing a video game.
When I spoke to Neurable earlier this year, the company said it planned to license its brain-scanning technology to power a flood of gadgets that were ready to enter the market. But it decided to launch its own hardware first.
“We wanted to take the product in-house,” Ramses Alcaide, Neurable’s cofounder and CEO, tells WIRED. “There were a lot of areas where we wanted to improve the product, and we wanted to move at a much faster rate. It also puts a little more capability for us to be able to show off what’s possible with the technology.”
The Boston company has until now relied on other brands to showcase its brain-scanning technology in their products, all of which promise to help people improve focus and provide data about your brain activity in a companion app. It began a few years ago by building its tech into some Master & Dynamic headphones. At the start of this year, Neurable showed off a gaming headset with HP's HyperX featuring two electroencephalography (EEG) sensors built in.
Like the original M&D MW75 Neuro headphones, the Neurable One features 12 EEG sensors in the nylon earpads that are used to monitor brain waves. The headphones cost $499 and will be available in October from Neurable’s website.
Alongside the new headphones is a new app (the old app will continue to exist for now for older hardware), which Alcaide says tracks eight brain metrics:
- Brain Age: Tracks your brain’s perceived age against your real age.
- Brain Battery: What you have left in reserve.
- Speed: How quickly you process information.
- Focus: How well your attention is holding.
- Load: How much effort you spend doing the task.
- Stress: How much tension you have doing the task.
- Sleepiness: How far you are drifting toward sleep.
- Alpha Peak Frequency: Your strongest resting rhythm, which Neurable claims is like the brain's heart rate variability.
The biggest hardware and software change with the Neurable One is that you no longer have to start a session in the app to capture brain activity. Instead, the Neurable One passively monitors your brain as soon as you put the headphones on—Alcaide likens it to wearing a Fitbit.
At that point, the sensors begin monitoring your brain activity to measure your focus. When it detects that you’re getting distracted, the headphones play a ping to get you back on track. If it thinks you're burning out instead, it’ll recommend a break so you can come back later fully recharged.
The headphone-app combo works similarly to help you fall asleep and to meditate. For example, with meditation, you can follow a guided session, and when the headphones detect you’re in the flow, the guide will stop talking so you stay in that zone. If it detects you’re drifting away, it’ll start guiding you back again. For sleep—designed for naps rather than proper bedtime—it can, over time, lower the headset volume of guided naps or soundscapes as it detects you falling asleep. (You can also turn off the EEG sensors and just use them as regular headphones if you want.)
Alcaide says when the app tells him his brain battery is low for the day, he’ll go to the sauna and go to bed early to help him recover. It can tell him when his peak brain speed hours are, allowing him to rejigger his schedule so he does his hardest work during those times. There’s also a check-in system called Cognitive Snapshot; when you trigger it, the app shows your current brain state and offers recommendations to improve it. That could be a guided meditation or small games to exercise those parts of your brain. The app also provides weekly or monthly reports to track your brain activity over time.
Neurable doesn’t have any new research or data to share that can speak to the effectiveness of its latest headphones. That research is in the works, but it will take time. So Neurable still points to previous research with the Mayo Clinic, which showed a 30 percent increase in focus in individuals using Neurable's headset versus people using Pomodoro techniques or other types of focus-sustaining systems. The study also saw a drop of about 10 percent in end-of-day burnout and an increase in end-of-day happiness.
The product isn’t categorized as a medical device, and Neurable says it isn’t designed to diagnose, treat, or monitor any conditions. The company also promises not to sell any of the data it collects about your brain—which could become very valuable in the future—and says it doesn't use that data for advertising. Alcaide says enterprise customers buy its headsets in bulk to help employees focus, but they’re not buying the headsets to monitor the workforce.
“It's because we know we're going to get higher productivity per employee; they're going to be happier, they're going to feel less burned out, it's a win-win for everybody,” he says. “It's like how sometimes companies get gym memberships for their employees.” He stresses that each user’s data stays with them.
Alcaide says the company partnered with an audio brand to help with the non-brain-scanning bits of the hardware, though he wouldn’t share the name. These cans have the “same premium sound” as the earlier M&D collaboration, with 40-mm beryllium drivers, six microphones, active noise cancellation, a transparency mode, and 22 hours of run time—12 if you have those EEG sensors running. It supports Bluetooth 5.2, and both AAC and aptX codecs. Neurable’s app is available on both Android and iOS.
articles.summary:
Neurable has launched the Neurable One, a $499 pair of brain-scanning headphones featuring 12 EEG sensors designed to monitor focus, stress, and cognitive load in real time.

### Key Points
- The Neurable One headphones feature 12 integrated EEG sensors that passively monitor brain activity without requiring manual app activation.
- The companion app tracks eight metrics, including brain age, focus, stress, and sleepiness, to provide personalized productivity and recovery recommendations.
- Hardware specifications include 40-mm beryllium drivers, active noise cancellation, and a battery life of up to 22 hours, or 12 hours with sensors active.
- The device will be available for purchase on the company's website starting in October for $499.
- Neurable states the product is not a medical device and commits to not selling user brain data or using it for advertising purposes.

### Why it Matters
This release marks a strategic shift for Neurable as it moves from licensing its brain-computer interface technology to third-party manufacturers to producing its own consumer hardware. By integrating passive monitoring into everyday audio gear, the company aims to normalize neuro-tracking as a tool for workplace productivity and personal wellness.

articles.title: I Tested the Three Big Voice Assistants to See Who’s Best at Predicting Weather
articles.author: Tyler Lacoma
articles.content:
Ever wonder which voice assistant knows your weather the best? For the past couple of months, I’ve been testing out the big three — Amazon’s Alexa Plus, Google Gemini for Home (which is busy replacing Google Assistant) and Apple’s Siri AI — to see who gets the weather right most often. They all pull their weather data from the internet, but their sources and algorithms lead to drastically different results.
Read more: Best Smart Speakers for 2026
My high desert city makes an excellent review location for weather reports, from the federal cuts to weather stations and forecast funding to our many microclimates coexisting under the Cascade Mountains. It’s the perfect spot for voice assistants to test their mettle, plus the online sources they draw their weather data from, allowing us to see which is accurate in tough conditions.
More from CNET
If you like asking your voice assistant about today’s weather as you prep for work, school or even camping plans, here are my real-world results, and which assistant ultimately proved best.
Alexa Plus: The chatty, overconfident relative
Wow, Alexa loves to chat. While the AI voice assistant has several personalities to pick from, mine is on the standard setting but frequently enjoys talking things out.
Not only does Alexa typically have the longest weather reports, but it also provides the most detail, for better and worse. Alexa Plus is the voice assistant to get extra tidbits about the wind level, snow advisories, air quality levels, chances of rain in the afternoon and other data, some more useful than others. The voice assistant also frequently makes asides, like explaining, “It’s 55 out but feels more like 65” due to the sun and lack of wind or other weather elements.
Exact weather predictions were generally accurate, but the assistant occasionally slipped up, such as predicting rain when none materialized. Alexa often overestimated the highs and lows in my area by a few degrees, too.
Amazon must have Alexa equipped with some sort of randomizer because none of this info is guaranteed, and the greetings and phrasing tend to change regularly. It’s fun, but it’s a little wild and not always accurate. A few times, Alexa tried to tell me my desert climate was at “99% humidity,” possibly because some online discussion about relative humidity got mixed in.
If you like extra info and don’t mind things being random, Alexa Plus may be your best pick, although the accuracy of its weather report isn’t always top-notch. Keep in mind, Alexa Plus is free with an Amazon Prime subscription but will otherwise cost around $20 per month. Also, while I tested the standard version of Alexa Plus, choosing different personalities or asking it to be more terse can help cut down on the info you get, so Alexa has plenty of customization options available here.
Read more: The Ultimate Guide to the Best Amazon Alexa Voice Commands
Gemini for Home: The no-nonsense reporter
Interestingly, Gemini on my Nest Hub narrowed results down to my exact neighborhood instead of the city as a whole. I don’t know how much this affected weather predictions, but Gemini proved the most accurate out of the voice assistants. Its highs and lows were typically accurate within a degree or two, and it didn’t overestimate like Alexa did. (If anything, it tended to undershoot the highs.)
While a quick “Hey Google” may yield the best weather reports, the voice assistant doesn’t provide much more info. Sometimes Gemini added info about overcast skies or rain, but nothing to the extent of Alexa.
If short and sweet is your preference, this is the most reliable option. I also like Gemini’s visuals best, with the forecast divided into hours so you can easily see when temperatures reach their height or when clouds are likely to move in.
Siri: The hesitant moderate
While not quite as formal as Gemini, Siri is likewise terse on weather reports and didn’t volunteer any extra info, like cloudy skies or rain, unless specifically asked in follow-up questions.
As for accuracy, Siri’s estimates were typically somewhere between Alexa’s slightly overblown expectations and Gemini’s more conservative approach, making it the moderate of the bunch.
That makes Siri a reasonable option for weather predictions, except I noticed what seemed like an odd bug where Apple’s voice assistant would suddenly forecast a high about five degrees higher than the other options and way off the mark. Sometimes it would do the same with lows, citing a temperature five degrees lower than what they actually reached.
I’m not sure why this discrepancy crept in, but it made Siri less reliable over time during my daily tests.
Bottom line
If you have an eye on accuracy and reliable weather reports when heading out in the morning, I recommend Gemini’s brief but good weather summaries. If you can get them on a smart display, like a Nest Hub, it also offers my favorite accompanying graphics.
Alexa Plus, however, wins for the sheer amount of information it provides and its chatty nature. You may never be sure what your weather report will include, but it’s likely to have a bit of everything, and you can ask Alexa to tone it down if need be.
Siri, meanwhile, had some issues suddenly overshooting or undershooting the mark and didn’t provide any helpful details, making it the least effective at handling your weather needs.
Who gives the most accurate current temperature readings?
Along with predictions, I also tested out voice assistant abilities to give current temperature readings. Since I have smart thermostats and plenty of portable air quality monitors from my testing, this was easy to double-check and see how they performed.
The voice assistants typically stayed within a couple of degrees of the temperature outside my house. In most cases, they were a degree or two lower, but nothing problematic.
The exception is Siri, where that odd bug estimating the temperature about five degrees higher than it was crept in once more. I couldn’t figure out what caused that bug, but it did make Siri occasionally wrong in contrast to the other voice assistants.
A final tip now that you have the lowdown on the weather: You can sync up weather reports, traffic reports, news and other tidbits in a single morning routine so voice assistants provide you with all this information at once, usually with a phrase like “Good morning.” It can be a timesaver — see my guide for more information.
articles.summary:
A recent performance test of Amazon’s Alexa Plus, Google Gemini for Home, and Apple’s Siri reveals significant differences in weather reporting accuracy and detail across smart voice assistants.

### Key Points
- Google Gemini for Home proved the most accurate, providing precise neighborhood-level forecasts and clear hourly visual data on Nest Hub devices.
- Amazon’s Alexa Plus offers the most comprehensive weather details, including wind and air quality, though its reports are occasionally inconsistent or overly chatty.
- Apple’s Siri performed as a moderate option but suffered from recurring bugs that caused temperature estimates to deviate by five degrees from actual conditions.
- All three assistants maintained reasonable accuracy for current temperature readings, generally staying within a few degrees of verified local monitors.
- Users can improve efficiency by syncing weather, traffic, and news updates into a single "Good morning" routine across these platforms.

### Why it Matters
Choosing the right voice assistant for daily planning depends on whether a user prioritizes granular data or high-precision accuracy. These performance variations highlight how different underlying algorithms and data sources impact the reliability of smart home devices for essential daily tasks.

articles.title: Thinking about a career pivot? A Google engineer shares what he learned from taking a leap of faith.
articles.author: Jacob Zinkula
articles.content:
This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Prerit Pathak, a 28-year-old security engineer at Google in New York City. It has been edited for length and clarity.
I think some people mistakenly believe that being a 'tech employee' is synonymous with being a software engineer. But I've always had a fascination for cybersecurity.
I vividly remember jailbreaking my devices as a kid to enhance their capabilities. Hacking for me meant making something do what it wasn't intended to do. It's the art of navigating edge cases — to question the builder's assumptions and make the supposedly impossible possible.
Despite that interest, I started my career as a software engineer at Dell Technologies in India.
Compared to software engineering or AI, I believe there's a lack of public-facing mentorship and "day-in-the-life" transparency with the cybersecurity field, which makes it harder for people looking to break in to see themselves in the role.
I believe the age of AI has created a strong demand for cybersecurity roles, and I'm glad I eventually found my way back to it.
Cybersecurity became more than a side interest
During my undergraduate degree, I sharpened my skills as a security researcher through classes, self-study, and participating in "Capture the Flag" challenges. But I was still trying to understand which career path I wanted to take.
When I got an offer for a software engineering job at Dell at the beginning of my senior year, it was a good opportunity, so I decided to accept it. My software engineering experience ended up being a great technical foundation for my career.
While working as a software engineer, I found a vulnerability on a public website and reported it to the website's management, with details on how to fix it. Eventually, through continuing that kind of work, I received appreciation letters and acknowledgments from top universities and organizations for disclosing critical vulnerabilities. Seeing the tangible impact of security research inspired me to pursue the field.
While I was working at Dell, I also set up a local chapter of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a cybersecurity nonprofit. As part of the chapter, I invited speakers from around the world to give talks.
At this point, I decided to go to graduate school at Carnegie Mellon University because I wanted to specialize and learn deeply about information security. Attending a top school like Carnegie Mellon meant being around people from whom I could learn, and I hoped it would help me transition into the cybersecurity field.
I moved to the US and eventually landed a job at Google
In 2021, I moved to the US to start graduate school and then completed a Google security engineering internship the following summer. I had a great internship, but my team didn't have an opening at my level, so I went back to school to finish my degree.
In 2023, two months after earning my master's degree, I joined Google full-time in New York.
My Google internship and graduate-school curriculum were important parts of my pivot, but I also think the things I did outside of that helped. I filed two patents, including one stemming from work I did with team members during my Google internship. These experiences, in addition to the appreciation letters I received, helped signal what I could do in security.
Now, as a security engineer, I create and run threat simulations to replicate adversary behavior in enterprise environments. The most time-consuming part of my job is usually analysis and reporting, which consists of analyzing the outcomes of the tests mentioned above, piecing observations together to form a coherent story, and finally reporting it.
Here's my advice for breaking into cybersecurity
Before getting hired at Google, I attended conferences, learned from mentors in the security industry, and applied to and was rejected by a few companies, learning from each. I'm a huge proponent of "failing forward." When you find and create opportunities for yourself, luck finds you.
For software engineers who want to shift to cybersecurity, like I did, I'd recommend using their technical skills to their advantage. As builders, they understand how those systems work; the pivotal shift in thinking is to understand how they can be taken advantage of.
Networking definitely has its role in uncovering opportunities, but preparing for and successfully navigating the interviews was, in my opinion, more crucial. I try to remember that an interview is a conversation between two people and that the interviewer is on your side. Asking clarifying questions before responding can improve your chances of giving a good answer. I'd also recommend thinking out loud so the interviewer can understand your thought process and, in some cases, nudge you in the right direction.
I'd suggest focusing on communication skills because stellar security engineers are empathetic partners who can convey technical risks to leadership without diluting the gravitas of any high-stakes situation.
I think it's also important to learn what working in cybersecurity actually looks like. When I was looking for jobs, it was hard to get insight into what careers in cybersecurity could look like. Connecting with others in the field helped me learn and build my own path.
Looking back, making the shift from software engineering to cybersecurity was a leap of faith. I'm incredibly grateful I made it.

articles.title: OpenAI Disrupts Reasoning Extraction Campaign Linked to Moonshot AI Associates
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
OpenAI on Wednesday said it identified and disrupted a coordinated distillation campaign that was designed to illicitly extract protected reasoning from its artificial intelligence (AI) models.
A "core cluster of the activity," going back to the first week of July, has been attributed to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, a Chinese AI company based in Beijing. It did not cite any technical evidence to back this assessment, likely owing to security reasons.
"The operators did not break our encryption, compromise a database, or gain direct access to stored user conversations," OpenAI said. "Instead, they manipulated model interactions so that protected reasoning could be reproduced in forms visible to the requester in a coordinated, scaled manner that violated our terms of service."
The activity is said to have begun on July 1, 2026, initially at a low volume before it spiked on July 24 and 25, 2026, to 16,000 attempted requests using a relevant extraction pattern from over 4,000 users. Upon further investigation, the company said it identified related "prompt-pattern activity" across more than 15,000 users. The campaign was fully disrupted on July 28, 2026.
The AI upstart characterized the activity as adversarial distillation, one that involves the systematic and unauthorized use of one model's outputs to help train, reproduce, or improve another model. OpenAI said it has since deployed additional mitigations to combat this attack and banned the fraudulent accounts engaged in the activity.
In addition, OpenAI said it closed a "pathway" that made it possible for someone who already possessed another user's encrypted reasoning to replay it and recover its contents, alongside adding checks to detect and hold streamed output that might expose reasoning.
In a study published in August 2026, a group of researchers found an architectural vulnerability impacting Claude, Gemini, and GPT that made the encrypted reasoning traces "fully compatible and interchangeable across different sessions, users, and models within a provider's ecosystem." An attacker could exploit this technicality to develop a scalable decryption jailbreak and circumvent anti-distillation mechanisms.
"By injecting an encrypted reasoning trace from a given model into a weaker, and less safeguarded model from the same provider, we force it to decode and output the trace verbatim in plaintext, without ever jailbreaking the more capable model directly," researchers from MATS Research, ELLIS Institute Tübingen, and Synk said.
Furthermore, it allows for large-scale private data extraction, opens the door for invisible prompt injections by embedding malicious payloads entirely within encrypted blocks, and inadvertently reveals hazardous information hidden within the reasoning process, even if the model's final, visible output rejects a harmful request.
Given that protected reasoning offers insights into how a model works its way through a task, extracting this information can reveal sensitive data and help others reproduce the model's capabilities, OpenAI added.
"Adversarial distillation poses safety and national security risks," the company said. "Extracted reasoning could be used to train another model without preserving the safeguards applied to the original model's user-facing outputs."
"At scale, distillation can also accelerate the transfer of advanced capabilities without requiring the same investment in safety. These concerns become heightened as models gain capabilities in dual-use domains."
This is not the first time Moonshot AI has faced distillation accusations. Last month, rival Anthropic accused Moonshot AI of stealthily relaying customer requests to Claude as opposed to processing them using Kimi, and then displaying responses from Claude back to the users.
The company is also alleged to have retained a subset of these exchanges to train its chain-of-thought (CoT) model. The activity has been tracked under the moniker GTG-16002.

OpenAI has disrupted a coordinated campaign by Beijing-based Moonshot AI that attempted to illicitly extract protected reasoning from its artificial intelligence models through adversarial distillation techniques.

### Key Points
- OpenAI identified and blocked a campaign that used over 15,000 user accounts to extract model reasoning between July 1 and July 28, 2026.
- The activity involved manipulating model interactions to reproduce protected reasoning, violating OpenAI’s terms of service.
- Researchers from MATS Research and the ELLIS Institute identified an architectural vulnerability allowing encrypted reasoning traces to be decrypted across different sessions.
- OpenAI implemented new mitigations and closed security pathways to prevent the replay of encrypted reasoning data.
- Moonshot AI previously faced similar accusations from Anthropic regarding the unauthorized use of Claude’s outputs to train its own models.

### Why it Matters
Adversarial distillation allows competitors to replicate advanced AI capabilities and safety protocols without the significant investment required for original model development. This practice poses serious national security risks by potentially bypassing safety guardrails and exposing sensitive data embedded within the reasoning process.

articles.title: Fixing The Back-Office Problem That Eats Into Agency Margins
articles.author: AdExchanger Content Studio
articles.content:
Don Draper would be overwhelmed by the sophistication of digital advertising. But he’d laugh at how unsophisticated financial reconciliation remains.
We can buy impressions in milliseconds and continuously optimize, yet, on the back end, we’re still exporting spreadsheets and manually reconciling invoices against contracts and delivery. The more sophisticated the front end gets, the less sustainable the reconciliation becomes.
This creates pain for accounting teams and economic friction for agencies. Manual work, meanwhile, erodes margins, and delayed billing means cash-flow pressure across the business (not to mention that it drives CFOs crazy).
Reconciliation is the symptom; fragmentation is the problem
The industry’s first wave of AI focused on optimization. Google optimized Google. Meta optimized Meta. DSPs optimized DSPs. The result was tremendous efficiency gains inside of individual systems. But AI did little to solve how those systems work together. In many cases, it accelerated fragmentation by making disconnected platforms operate faster.
Amid the growing media complexity, agencies ultimately need to know: What was contracted? Planned? Bought? Delivered? What did each platform report? What did the publisher invoice? And what should the client be billed?
Answers to those questions live in different systems, and financial reconciliation is where all those versions of reality finally must become one. When that data doesn’t move automatically between systems, people become the connective tissue by exporting files, compiling spreadsheets and manually investigating the almost-inevitable discrepancies.
Say an impression is contracted at $10 but comes through reporting at $11. Now the agency has to determine which number is correct, where the discrepancy originated and what the client and vendor should actually be charged.
The cost of manual reconciliation
1. Expensive human labor eats into profitability.
Manual data aggregation is costly on its own, but the more expensive part is the manual investigation to determine why two (or more) systems disagreed in the first place. Discrepancies are constant. When agencies need more employee hours to administer the same media spend, their service cost goes up and margins go down.
2. Slow reconciliation creates cash-flow problems.
Multifaceted campaigns can take weeks or months to reconcile, delaying billing and collection. If an agency owes a publisher before receiving payment from the advertiser, it effectively becomes a bank for its client, sometimes needing to draw on lines of credit and paying interest while waiting for cash to come in. This is the stuff of CFO nightmares.
3. Payment delays ripple through the media supply chain.
These payment delays propagate downstream to publishers and other media partners. In some large agency relationships, payment terms stretch as long as 120 or 150 days, creating the same wave of cash-flow pressures within the publisher world.
Consolidation doesn’t make sense
Large vendors have a traditional answer for fragmentation: Consolidate everything into one platform (aka ours). But this doesn’t fit agency reality today.
With technology advancing so quickly and completely new capabilities appearing at a rapid rate, agencies see best-of-breed strategy as the only way to remain competitive.
The answer, then, can’t be forcing agencies to choose between having the best tech for the job and having manageable back-end operations. The future won’t be won by the platform that replaces everything. Rather, it will be won by the platform that connects everything.
Orchestration offers a new path
Leading agencies are building a new kind of “AI orchestration layer” to resolve fragmentation across their core operations, connecting data and workflows across planning, activation, measurement and actualization. This leaves agencies free to fully embrace a best-of-breed strategy.
Historically, those functions operated as discrete steps, with reconciliation sitting at the end. Orchestration creates a more continuous information flow. Instead of manually reconstructing a campaign at month-end, an orchestration layer can pull together the relevant data continuously, identify discrepancies earlier and coordinate the information needed to resolve them.
That makes financial reconciliation less of a standalone process and more the byproduct of a well-run system.
Tech vendors are supporting this agentic enterprise model through new partnerships. For example, the integration between Basis and Mediaocean Prisma brings together planning, activation and actualized omnichannel campaign data, then passes that clean data set into Prisma for financial reconciliation and invoicing. Changes in Prisma can flow back into Basis as well, helping both systems operate from a consistent source of truth.
Better agency economics
Removing repetitive manual work reduces the labor required to administer the same media spend.
But an even bigger economic boon could come from better visibility. A continuously orchestrated approach gives agencies a much clearer view of accounts payable and receivable – what clients owe, what publishers are owed and where discrepancies remain – so they can understand how cash moves through the business.
There may even be a strategic upside. Agencies with clean accounts receivable and accounts payable and a track record of paying partners quickly can have more leverage to negotiate favorable payment and credit terms with vendors.
The next frontier of AI is orchestration
This story is part of a broader emerging trend. Some of the most valuable applications of AI in advertising may be around the administrative work that keeps campaigns moving by coordinating repetitive workflows, connecting fragmented data and, now, orchestrating financial reconciliation.
This isn’t flashy, but it is consequential. It’s about how healthier cash flow supports a healthier marketplace.
The first generation of AI helped marketers make better decisions. The next generation will help agencies run better businesses.
For more articles featuring Michael Olson, click here.
articles.summary:
Digital advertising agencies are increasingly adopting AI orchestration layers to automate complex financial reconciliation processes, reducing manual labor costs and improving cash flow across the media supply chain.

### Key Points
- Manual reconciliation of fragmented data across multiple advertising platforms creates significant administrative costs and erodes agency profit margins.
- Delayed billing cycles force agencies to act as temporary banks for clients, often leading to cash-flow pressures and reliance on credit lines.
- Payment delays ripple through the industry, sometimes extending vendor payment terms to as long as 150 days.
- Agencies are moving away from platform consolidation in favor of "best-of-breed" technology stacks that prioritize interoperability.
- New AI orchestration tools, such as the integration between Basis and Mediaocean Prisma, connect planning, activation, and financial data to create a single source of truth.

### Why it Matters
Automating back-end financial operations allows agencies to maintain competitive, specialized technology stacks without sacrificing operational efficiency. By streamlining these workflows, firms can improve their bottom line and gain the financial leverage necessary to negotiate better terms with media partners.

articles.title: Closed foldables cause Android Auto calls to fail: Moto and Google are investigating
articles.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Users with Android Auto in their cars report that, if their foldable is closed, the system will fail to place a call unless they open it.
- Several reports involve Motorola's Razr series, but Gemini has also been mentioned heavily in a series of online reports.
- Motorola and Google are aware and are reaching out to users for information.
Drivers beware: A fresh Android Auto bug seems to be unfolding. The issue has drawn increased attention this week regarding a call failure bug — and user reports on social media and official OEM forums claim that the state of their foldable is the cause.
Reports are spread across Reddit, Google's Forums, and Motorola's (via Android Authority). A user reported this issue on Reddit a few months back, stating they're unable to make a call through Android Auto when their Moto Razr Ultra 2025 is closed. They must open it before their call can be placed. They questioned whether this is the result of Android 16, but that doesn't appear to be the case.
Others chimed in, reiterating the same issue as the OP. A report on the Google forums sheds more light: It states that "ever since Gemini became active," attempting to place a call while the user's foldable is closed will result in an Android Auto failure. The post adds, "it pulls up the person and phone number, but doesn't process the call."
These reports share something in common: closed foldable results in failure and Gemini's wider rollout. The timing is far too close for comfort, and it seems some users clocked this, too. Back on Reddit, one user discovered that if they disabled Gemini and reverted to the old Google Assistant, their calls would go through, regardless of whether their foldable was opened or closed.
While concerning, the publication noticed that Motorola and Google have been active and watching these reports. It looks like both companies are aware of what's going on with Gemini and with the Razr foldables. All we have to do now is wait for a fix.
Android Auto woes continue
This is such a weird problem to have that it's almost funny. It's not like we have to keep our foldables open for calls outside of the car. Could you imagine that though? It would be like holding a tablet up to your ear. My jokes aside, let's hope Motorola and Google can figure out where the issue lies and fix it for good.
Android Auto has its issues (no one's denying that). There was a problem with the Pixel 10 that users encountered when connecting the device. According to user reports, a gray screen would appear when their phone was connected to Android Auto. What's more, there was a freezing issue that didn't get fixed when Google rolled out a patch. Elsewhere, Android Auto users had a problem in March with the signal icon.
This wasn't as terrible as what some are facing today. The signal icon for cellular connectivity was disappearing on the car's display. In short, it was a UI bug. Users reported that everything else worked perfectly fine: connectivity, calls, data, and navigation. The problem was linked back to Android Auto version 16.5. Users found relief by reverting to an older version.
