articles.title: Samsung has updated these Galaxy devices to Android 17
articles.author: Ben Schoon
articles.content:
Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update.
What’s new in Android 17 on Samsung Galaxy?
One UI 9, Samsung’s Android 17 update, continues the trend of evolution more than overhaul. The update introduces some slight design tweaks, more AI-powered features, and other changes built on the redesign that debuted in One UI 7 and was iterated in last year’s Android 16-based One UI 8.
Some key changes in One UI 9 include:
- Warranty & Samsung Care status in the Settings menu
- Broader support for Now Nudge
- My FanCam automatic video cropping based on a select subject
- More Quick Panel (quick settings) customization
- AI privacy alerts
- Upgrades to Samsung DeX
- New lock screen clocks that can adapt to your wallpaper
Samsung Galaxy devices with Android 17 – The full list
While Samsung hasn’t confirmed an exact schedule for its One UI 9 and Android 17 rollout for Galaxy devices, there are updates now rolling out in parts of the globe. Below you’ll find a regularly-updated list of every Samsung Galaxy device that has received a stable Android 17 update so far.
Galaxy S devices with Android 17
- Galaxy S26
- Galaxy S26+
- Galaxy S26 Ultra
- Galaxy S25 (limited availability)
- Galaxy S25+ (limited availability)
- Galaxy S25 Ultra (limited availability)
- Galaxy S25 FE (limited availability)
- Galaxy S25 Edge (limited availability)
Galaxy Z devices with Android 17
- Galaxy Z Fold 7 (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z Flip 7 (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE (limited availability)
- Galaxy Z TriFold (limited availability)
Updating…
One UI 9 changelog
Here’s the full changelog from Samsung for One UI 9, as listed for the Galaxy S26 series. Some features may vary by device.
Galaxy AI
Enhanced Now nudge
- Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.
Focus on someone important
- My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.
Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you
- In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.
See useful information during calls
- See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.
Productivity and multitasking
More customizable quick panel
- You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.
Privacy, security, and device protection
Warranty and care
- The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.
Lock down your phone quickly
- It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.
Location access transparency
- Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.
Stronger security and privacy protection
- Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.
AI privacy alerts
- Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.
Samsung Health
New look for Samsung Health
- Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.
Customize your Health home screen
- Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.
Log health data quickly
- It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.
Advanced trend analysis
- Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.
Monitor changes in your sleep vitals
- Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.
Manage your heart health
- Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.
Track your cardio load
- See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.
Check your fitness index
- Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.
Keep your ears safe
- The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.
View your cycle and body rhythm
- Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.
Bixby
Activate Bixby with a gesture
- Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.
Manage your conversations
- Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.
Bixby on the Home screen
- Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.
Accessibility
Discover new Accessibility features
- Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.
Text spotlight for easier reading
- Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.
Physical keyboard shortcuts
- Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.
Mouse keys enhancements
- New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.
Replace swipe with single tap
- The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.
Select to speak
- Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.
Improved TalkBack updates
- TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.
Even more improvements
New Lock screen clock
- The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.
Samsung DeX enhancements
- It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.

articles.title: Product showcase: Proton Drive end-to-end encrypted cloud storage
articles.author: Anamarija Pogorelec
articles.content:
Product showcase: Proton Drive end-to-end encrypted cloud storage
Proton Drive is an end-to-end encrypted cloud storage service for storing, synchronizing, backing up, and sharing files. It also includes Proton Docs and Proton Sheets, allowing users to create and collaborate on documents and spreadsheets within the same encrypted environment.
Proton Drive is available through the web and dedicated apps for Windows, macOS, iOS/iPadOS, and Android. Proton also offers a command-line interface for Windows, macOS, and Linux.
After signing in or creating a Proton Account, the app opens into a familiar file-management interface with separate areas for Files, Photos, Computers, and items shared with the user.
Files across devices
On macOS, Proton Drive integrates directly with Finder and appears under Locations. Files can be handled much like those in an ordinary Mac folder. Cloud files can remain online and be downloaded when needed, while those that need to be accessible without a connection can be kept locally.
On the iPhone, the app provides access to files and folders, with options to upload and organize content, create folders and documents, and make files available offline. Automatic photo and video backup is also available.
Encryption is at the center
Proton Drive encrypts files on the user’s device before they are uploaded. Proton says it cannot access the contents of files protected this way. The service also uses cryptographic signatures to protect file authenticity, while its applications are open source and independently audited.
Users can share files and folders through links or directly with other people, with controls including permissions, password protection, expiration dates, and the ability to revoke access.
Final thoughts
During my testing, moving between the Mac and iPhone was simple. Files uploaded to Drive were available from both devices, while Finder integration made the desktop experience feel similar to working with local files.
articles.summary:
Proton Drive provides a secure, end-to-end encrypted cloud storage platform that enables users to synchronize, back up, and collaborate on files across web, desktop, and mobile operating systems.

### Key Points
- Proton Drive features integrated tools for document and spreadsheet creation, including Proton Docs and Proton Sheets.
- The service is compatible with Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android, featuring native Finder integration on Mac devices.
- Files are encrypted locally on the user's device before upload, ensuring that Proton cannot access stored content.
- Security measures include cryptographic signatures, open-source application code, and independent third-party audits.
- Sharing features allow users to set password protection, expiration dates, and specific access permissions for individual files or folders.

### Why it Matters
This service offers a privacy-focused alternative to mainstream cloud providers by ensuring that user data remains inaccessible to the service provider. Its cross-platform functionality and document collaboration tools provide a comprehensive ecosystem for users prioritizing data security in their digital workflows.

articles.title: Data Centers Are a $6 Trillion Time Bomb, Analysts Warn
articles.author: Joe Wilkins
articles.content:
Last year, hedge fund whisperer and founder of the firm Praetorian Capital, Harris Kupperman, issued a blistering financial analysis on the data center frenzy sweeping across the United States.
Kupperman’s diagnosis was blunt: because data center components break down so quickly, the industry would need to see some $1 trillion in revenue across 2025 and 2026 just to cover the costs of their hyperscale facilities, let alone start turning a profit. With AI revenue today accounting for only a small fraction of that total, Kupperman’s argument is that the financial logic behind the data center buildout simply doesn’t hold up.
But as the last year has shown us, the magnates of the AI industry — and their funders — have a remarkable knack for kicking the can down the road, no matter how bad the numbers might look. That being the case, analysts are starting to use Kupperman’s same rationale to forecast what the next few years have in store for data center developers — and the numbers are staggering.
As Bloomberg reports, an analysis on data centers by Bain and Co, one of the largest management consulting firms in the world, found that the global AI industry would have to reach annual revenue of $6 trillion by 2031 to justify the amount of capital being injected into data centers.
The analysis assumes that commercial AI tools will account for $1.8 trillion of revenue by that point — a pretty generous presumption, which requires global AI revenue to start growing almost exponentially. Even if the AI industry reaches that point, Bain’s analysis notes, the industry will still need to come up with $4.2 trillion.
Hitting that $6 trillion mark will take nothing short of a technological miracle, the report authors explain, a leap without precedent in the information age.
“What the industry needs is a wave of innovation that will dwarf what mobile and cloud unlocked,” the report’s lead author and chairman of Bain’s Global Technology, Media, and Telecommunications, David Crawford wrote.
“AI infrastructure is being built well ahead of the demand curve and funding it sustainably will require adding approximately one percent to the annual global GDP growth rate,” Bain’s report continues. “The question is whether the applications arrive in time to pay for it.”
Given that data centers are one of the few growth-areas in the US economy — Bain notes major hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle could spend up to $780 billion across 2026 alone — the domestic AI industry can’t afford to waver, no matter how unlikely that $6 trillion threshold may seem.
At the same time, tech giants can’t keep deploying capital forever, as Kupperman observed in his 2025 essay.
“If the economics don’t work, doing it at massive scale doesn’t make the economics work any better — it just takes an industry crisis and makes it into a national economic crisis,” he wrote.
So unless the tech industry can find a way to turn AI into a trillion-dollar revenue stream fast, it seems data centers are just a ticking time bomb waiting to go off. As Jessica Wachter, a finance professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School opined in a recent research paper, if this AI miracle “fails to materialize,” future generation will look back at the current buildout “as the largest misallocation of capital in history.”

A new report from Bain and Co suggests the global AI industry must reach $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify current data center infrastructure investments.

### Key Points

- Major hyperscalers including Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle may spend up to $780 billion on data centers in 2026 alone.

The parent company of the Texas Stock Exchange raised $155 million in a third funding round, bolstering its financial firepower as it challenges the New York Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq for equities listings.
TXSE Group Inc.’s existing shareholders are providing about three-quarters of the new money, with the rest coming from new backers. Funding for the exchange now totals $430 million, the Dallas-based company said in a statement Wednesday. It didn’t identify the new investors.
“Real competition for primary listings is here, and it is here to stay,” James Lee, TXSE’s founder and chief executive officer, said in the statement. The latest funding is an “institutional validation” of demand for a competing exchange, he said.
The TXSE, which won authorization from federal regulators a year ago, recently lured an initial slate of primary listings consisting largely of companies with close ties to the exchange. One of the most prominent is Energy Transfer LP, whose chairman, Kelcy Warren, owns a big stake in TXSE Group. Another is Texas Capital Bancshares Inc., which is led by Rob Holmes, a member of an advisory board to the exchange.
TXSE built its early pitch in part around support from big-name backers, attracting investments from the likes of BlackRock Inc. and Citadel Securities. It followed that up with a second round of fundraising led by JPMorgan Chase & Co.
The NYSE and Nasdaq, which have long dominated the competition for US listings, have responded to the threat with Texas-based venues designed to expand their reach in the state. Lee said TXSE’s focus would help it win new business.
“While the legacy equities exchanges prioritize fintech, prediction and energy markets, mortgages, data businesses and other pursuits, TXSE is solely focused on being the best exchange operator in the world,” he said.
Photo: The ceremonial gold bell that was rung to open the Texas Stock Exchange in Dallas on Sept. 9.

### Key Points
- TXSE Group Inc. raised $155 million, with existing shareholders contributing approximately 75% of the new capital.
- The company has reached a total of $430 million in funding to support its operations as a national securities exchange.
- Early primary listings include Energy Transfer LP and Texas Capital Bancshares Inc., both of which have leadership ties to the exchange.
- Major financial backers of the project include BlackRock Inc., Citadel Securities, and JPMorgan Chase & Co.
- The exchange aims to compete directly with the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq by focusing exclusively on equities trading.

### Why it Matters
The emergence of the Texas Stock Exchange represents a significant challenge to the long-standing dominance of the NYSE and Nasdaq in the U.S. equities market. By securing substantial institutional backing, the exchange is positioning itself as a viable alternative for companies seeking primary listings outside of traditional financial hubs.

articles.title: Nothing Is On Fire At Google via @sejournal, @pedrodias
articles.author: Pedro Dias
articles.content:
In February, Gemini 3.1 Pro sat at the top of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. It beat Claude Opus 4.6 by four points and cost less than half as much to run. For a few weeks, Google led on every chart the AI crowd likes to screenshot.
At I/O in May, Google promised Gemini 3.5 Pro for June. It didn’t arrive. In mid-July, Bloomberg reported that the model’s coding was short of where Google wanted it, and that an attempt to fix this by changing the training data had disappointed. Google’s statement talked about shipping many models quickly and keeping them “highly cost-effective for customers.”
Fair enough on the first part. Since July, Google has shipped Gemini 3.7 Flash, 3.8 Flash, speech models, a video model, a music model and a robotics model. Its API changelog, latest entry dated 22 September, still has no 3.5 Pro. In his Q2 earnings remarks, Sundar Pichai was already talking about Gemini 4 and “our most ambitious pre-training run yet.”
Yesterday I wrote on LinkedIn that I think Google’s chances of leading in AI are slim. Coming from me, that’s a change of position. I’ve bet on Google for years, and I always expected it to win this race. When the AI hype started, I was the cautious one, happy to let the novelty settle before jumping in.
I’m still cautious. I just don’t want to be blind to what’s in front of me. After 20 years in search, what I see in Google’s recent moves is a company turning into Microsoft: rich, everywhere, and slow to act against the business that pays for everything.
The replies to my post were good, and most of them disagreed. Almost all made the same case: Google owns the data and the distribution, makes its own chips, and has more cash than anyone it competes with.
All true. Microsoft had the cash and the distribution too.
I’m not predicting Google’s fall. Google will be fine. My argument is narrower: I don’t think Google has the motivation or the nerve to build the thing most likely to eat its search business, because the search business still works. The question was always whether Google is willing to break something that prints money.
Everything on the inventory is real
Let’s give the other side its full due. Google crawls the web, runs Chrome and Android, owns YouTube and sells Workspace to businesses. Its cloud backlog stood at $514 billion at the end of Q2. The Gemini app passed a billion monthly users in August, and Pichai says AI Mode has passed a billion too.
The strongest point against me comes from Comscore. On its US panel, Gemini’s share of AI assistant prompts went from 17% in January to 30% in June, while ChatGPT fell from 70% to 50%. That’s more than Gemini appearing in front of people. People are typing into it.
I accept all of it. An inventory tells you what a company can do. What it will choose to do is a separate question, and for that you watch where the scarce stuff goes.
Follow the chips
The scarce stuff in AI is compute. Google makes its own, and it rents it out. In May, The Information reported that Anthropic had committed to spend $200 billion over five years on Google’s cloud and chips. In Q2, Google Cloud revenue grew 82% to $24.8 billion, with operating income of $8.8 billion.
Now put that next to a Reuters exclusive from August. Tight computing capacity, and disputes between the people running different parts of Gemini, left areas such as coding short of resources. Cloud’s senior leaders, Reuters reported, hoped the new Gemini leadership would calm a fight with DeepMind over who gets Google’s limited chips. In April, The Information reported on a memo in which Sergey Brin told DeepMind staff that Google must “urgently bridge the gap” with Claude on agentic coding.
I don’t know how those allocation meetings went. I know how the quarter ended: Cloud up 82%, and the in-house model short of its coding targets.
As a business decision, it’s hard to argue with. A TPU rented to Anthropic is revenue this quarter. A TPU spent on another Gemini training run is a bet. That’s exactly my point. A company that must win takes the bet. A company already winning on the P&L takes the contract.
Search got an AI bodyguard
The same pattern shows on Google’s most valuable surface. When Google put generative AI into Search, it put it inside the results page: AI Overviews on top, AI Mode beside it, and ads moving into both. I covered what that means for publishers in Half Your Traffic Left: your content, consumed on Google’s surface, next to Google’s ads.
From Google’s side, it’s working. Search and other revenue grew 17% in Q2, to $63.3 billion, and Pichai credits the AI features with driving query growth. A defence that pays that well is the most comfortable place a company can be. Comfort is the problem.
What I think threatens Search is the assistant that does the job and never shows a results page at all. It writes the code, compares the contracts, books the trip, and nobody clicks an ad on the way. That’s the category where Google is furthest behind, and I don’t think that’s a coincidence. Building it properly means building the thing that makes Search optional. Every incentive inside Google points the other way.
Microsoft already ran this experiment
If distribution were enough, Microsoft would be winning. It had Windows, Edge and Office as default placement. It moved first, putting OpenAI’s technology into Bing in February 2023, while Google was still in its code red over ChatGPT.
Three and a half years later, Bing holds 4.5% of worldwide search, according to StatCounter’s August figures. Copilot, sitting right there in Windows, sends 2.8% of the AI chatbot referral traffic StatCounter tracks. StatCounter counts referral clicks rather than usage, so treat the Copilot number as rough. The direction isn’t in doubt.
Microsoft is fine, of course. It rents cloud compute to the companies building models, OpenAI among them. Sound familiar? Microsoft did very well selling shovels, and nobody calls it the leader in search or consumer AI. It failed to stay competitive on exactly the fronts that demanded it disrupt itself.
So what about Gemini’s consumer gains? They’re real, and they’re happening where Google’s distribution is strongest. Where people pick a model for paid work, the picture changes. Menlo Ventures’ 2025 enterprise report put Anthropic at 40% of enterprise LLM API spend, OpenAI at 27% and Google at 21%. In coding, it had Anthropic at 54% and OpenAI at 21%, with Google at 11%. Menlo is one of Anthropic’s biggest backers and co-runs a fund with it, so read those numbers with that in mind. Even with that discount applied, the money teams spend on getting work done has mostly gone elsewhere.
Google moves when something is on fire
To be fair, Google can move fast when it’s frightened. ChatGPT triggered a code red inside Google in December 2022. Two months later, Bard’s launch demo got a fact wrong and Alphabet shed about $100 billion in market value in a day. The recovery that followed was real. Gemini 2.5 Pro reached the top of LMArena in March 2025, and after Gemini 3, it was Sam Altman calling a code red at OpenAI.
So yes, Google can sprint. It needs a fright first. You could read the 3.5 Pro delay as Google being careful after Bard, and I’d accept that. Holding back a model that misses your own bar is discipline.
It just tells you nothing about whether Google will build the assistant that makes the results page optional. Nobody declares a code red when Search revenue is up 17%. Without a fire, Google moves at Microsoft speed.
Moving like Microsoft
Twenty years in search teach you to watch how a company moves, more than what it announces. Google’s announcements are fine. Its movements this year: a Pro model promised for June that still hasn’t shipped at the end of September, a coding gap its own co-founder flagged in April and a leadership reshuffle that only came in August, and a CEO talking up Gemini 4 before 3.5 Pro is out. To me, that’s the pace of a company protecting a lead. It’s the pace Microsoft had with Bing.
We’ve seen this before. Google had Gmail, Android, YouTube and most people’s contacts when it launched Google+ in 2011. It shut the consumer version in 2019. Google had every advantage in social except a need to win it. Go back further and you get Xerox PARC, which built the graphical interface and watched other companies ship it. Google researchers published the transformer paper in 2017. OpenAI turned it into ChatGPT.
The people seem to read the room the same way. Noam Shazeer, co-lead of Gemini, left for OpenAI in June. In August, Jeff Dean left after 27 years to co-found Discovery Loop, Demis Hassabis stepped back to chair DeepMind, and Koray Kavukcuoglu took direct control of Gemini. Fortune, using Zeki Data, reports that DeepMind’s hires per departure fell from roughly 12 in 2023 to roughly two now. Anthropic managed 22 in 2025. My read: researchers who want to build what comes next go where what comes next is the whole business.
What would change my mind
Two signals. The first is a Gemini product that does the job end to end, with no results page and no ad slot, pushed by Google as hard as it pushes AI Mode. The second is Google letting that product take queries away from Search, and saying so on an earnings call as if it were good news. If I see either, I’ll write the follow-up and eat my words.
Until then, Google will do fine. So did Microsoft. Ask Bing.

Google’s dominance in the AI sector faces scrutiny as internal resource allocation and a focus on protecting search revenue potentially hinder the development of disruptive, autonomous assistant technologies.

### Key Points
- Google has delayed the release of Gemini 3.5 Pro, missing its original June target while prioritizing cloud revenue and existing search-based AI features.
- Internal competition for limited compute resources between Google Cloud and the Gemini development team has reportedly hampered progress in key areas like coding.
- Despite strong consumer adoption of Gemini, enterprise data shows competitors like Anthropic and OpenAI currently lead in professional API spending and coding tasks.
- High-profile talent departures, including co-lead Noam Shazeer, suggest a shift in researcher sentiment toward companies where AI innovation is the primary business focus.
- Google’s search revenue grew 17% in Q2, reinforcing a corporate strategy that favors incremental improvements over radical disruption of its core advertising business.

### Why it Matters
Google’s current strategy mirrors Microsoft’s historical approach of prioritizing existing, profitable business lines over the development of potentially cannibalistic, next-generation technologies. This cautious pace may leave the company vulnerable to competitors who are willing to build autonomous agents that bypass traditional search interfaces entirely.

articles.title: The Real Existential Risk Is AI CEOs Avoiding Oversight: "Alternative Nobel" Winner Timnit Gebru
articles.author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
articles.content:
We speak to the prominent AI researcher and leading critic of the AI industry, Timnit Gebru, who was recently awarded a 2026 Right Livelihood Award for her work investigating the harms and hype behind the global buildup of artificial intelligence.
“Instead of discussing faulty, unreliable systems,” Gebru says tech leaders like SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei are “marketing their systems as all-knowing, superpowerful, superintelligent,” and lobbying for “self-policing and self-regulation” to avoid being held “liable through existing laws.” Gebru expresses skepticism over increasingly widespread claims that AI algorithms pose an existential risk to humanity, warning that such claims are overblown and that “what is actually happening is regulatory capture.”
Transcript
NERMEEN SHAIKH: On Tuesday, President Trump and leading tech and AI executives signed a set of voluntary safety standards for artificial intelligence. Trump announced the agreement at the White House alongside SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Google’s Sundar Pichai and others.
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: These are the most brilliant people in the world, and the job they’ve done is unbelievable. We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead. And it’s a very positive thing. It’s an amazing industry. There are those that say it’s bigger than the Industrial Revolution. Now, I don’t know if that’s so, but everyone seems to think it is, and it could be substantially bigger. And we’re leading, and we’re going to keep it that way.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: The White House meeting came after weeks of warnings from AI companies about their own products. In early September, an Anthropic researcher named Jacob Coxon resigned and warned that there’s more than a 10% chance AI could kill all humans. Anthropic has warned investors that advanced AI could pose, quote, “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” But the claims and motivations of the leading AI firms have also been questioned by some.
AMY GOODMAN: We begin today’s show with a leading critic of the AI industry, Timnit Gebru. She’s an AI researcher and the founder and executive director of the Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, or DAIR. Prior to that, she served as co-lead of the ethical AI research team at Google. She was fired in 2020 for writing a paper warning about the dangers of large language models and raising issues of discrimination in the workplace. Timnit Gebru also co-founded Black in AI. Her forthcoming book is titled Deep Unlearning: The Rise of AI and the Radicalization of a Tech Idealist.
On Wednesday, Timnit Gebru received the 2026 — it was announced she’s receiving the 2026 Right Livelihood Award, known as the Alternative Nobel. In a moment, she’ll join us. But first, this is a short video produced by Right Livelihood.
TIMNIT GEBRU: Most people think that AI is an existential risk.
MATTHEW AMROLIWALA: There is a 10% chance AI will kill us all in the next decade. It’s pretty clear why that statement has worried so many people.
SAM ALTMAN: If this technology goes wrong, it can go quite wrong.
TIMNIT GEBRU: But it’s actually the people who are building it that are the existential risks to humanity. If a bridge collapses, we don’t ever ask, “Was the bridge uncontrollable? Was the bridge unethical?” And really, AI is no different than that. When we describe these systems and artifacts like they have their own agency, we’re at the very same time helping the companies market themselves. But more importantly, what we’re doing is we’re also helping them sidestep accountability.
I’m a scientist trying to just do science, but it’s not possible in our world to just do that. Ten years ago, I was focused on changing the minds of powerful people, whereas now I’m focused on building grassroots power. The institute that I created, DAIR, we have technologists, we have refugee advocates, we have labor organizers, we have artists, and we also collaborate a lot with other people. I’ve been able to create a safe space for people like this to make their mark on technology and also imagine and reimagine what it means to build technology. What motivates me to keep going is the belief that we have to try to make things better, and I really do believe in human agency, and I believe in the ability of collective action. We can change things.
AMY GOODMAN: That’s a video produced by Right Livelihood profiling AI expert Timnit Gebru, who joins us now from Menlo Park, California.
Timnit, congratulations on the Right Livelihood Award prize. And I’m wondering if we can move right into the content you’ve been most focused on. Your response to President Trump and the world’s wealthiest tech executives signing a voluntary set of safety standards for artificial intelligence this week? If you can talk about your response and what’s happening right now in California, the major meeting that you’re attending?
TIMNIT GEBRU: Well, so, you know, I have been warning that this kind of discussion about the fictional superintelligent machines that don’t exist and the so-called existential risks that they pose has been a ploy for regulatory capture. And I feel like when I saw this meeting announced, with self-policing and self-regulation and relying on the goodwill of these companies to self-regulate, and I — my first thought was that they got what they wanted. You know, this is what they wanted, instead of being held liable through existing laws.
I mean, for example, if you wanted to look at cybersecurity laws, OpenAI could have been held liable for unleashing malware around the world, hacking Hugging Face, hacking all sorts of government agencies, but instead of doing that and holding them accountable for unsafe security practices that they should have had, basic security practices that cybersecurity experts would tell you they could have implemented, instead of that, they managed to redirect the conversation to some type of unprecedented rogue machines that don’t exist, and then now that leads to this kind of agreement between all these men, who I believe are the actual real existential risks to humanity, to self-regulate, self-police, and we have to rely on their morality now.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And if you could respond, Timnit, to the fact that the other tech executives all came down quite hard on Amodei of Anthropic, saying that he’s being too extreme in his public statements about the risks of AI?
TIMNIT GEBRU: Yeah, he is very extreme, but they’re no different. So, I’m not really — you know, maybe they’re saying now that he’s being too extreme, and so that might be changing investor responses. But all of them have, at one point or another, claimed that AI is an existential risk to humanity. Going back all the way to 2012, Elon Musk said that with AI we’re summoning the demon. In 2013, Peter Thiel said that AI is a higher existential risk to humanity than climate change. 2023, Sam Altman was talking about how his own creation is an existential risk.
But the difference, I think, what people really need to understand, is at the same time as these tech executives are saying that, in the same breath they also tell us that their products, the beneficial kind of AI, the kind of AI that they control because they’re the good guys, can eradicate poverty, stop climate change — which is ridiculous, because the data centers are actually causing climate catastrophe — and eradicate all disease. I mean, they’re in the same breath saying this. So, this is still, to me — the utopia and doom is still a marketing ploy. But maybe one of them went a little too far and is spooking investors, whereas in the past it was speaking to these defense capabilities.
In your headline, you talked about how the U.S. military is trying to integrate AI into every facet of its practices. And there was just a CNN investigative report that showed that the U.S. almost started World War III with China, relying on a faulty, fabricated information from a chatbot. Now, we don’t know which chatbot they used, but it’s obviously one of these providers. And this chatbot provided fake information saying that a Chinese vessel was carrying components of nuclear weapons. And the military was ready with planes, soldiers to intercept the ship, board the ship, and this was going to cause an actual existential threat to humanity.
So, now instead of discussing faulty, unreliable systems, we are — they are marketing their systems as all-knowing, superpowerful, superintelligent. So, regardless of how far Amodei may have gone in their eyes, all of them have been talking about their creations and products in that way.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: And, Timnit, if you could say — you know, you said earlier that it’s a ploy for regulatory capture and that, you know, these agents, as people describe them going rogue — although I understand that that’s not an accurate description — that these agents doing something reportedly different from what they were tasked to do is a result of unsafe practices. So, if you could talk about the regulatory capture question, and then what security practices, safety practices are in place that — or are there any in place?
TIMNIT GEBRU: Well, if you speak to any cybersecurity expert, they would tell you that whatever they had in place that they claim to have, the security practices, were laughable. For example, OpenAI was testing the capabilities of their models to find vulnerabilities and exploit them. That is what they trained these models to do, and they were testing the ability of these models to do what they were trained for. But the thing is, if you want to test this and you don’t want to hack other organizations, you should do it in what’s called an air-gapped environment, where there’s no internet access. And so, they did not have a properly air-gapped environment, and so the models ended up being able to have internet access. This is not models going rogue. This is gross incompetence and negligence by a particular company, which actually they could be held criminally liable for.
Lina Khan outlined a whole bunch of ways in which these companies can be currently held liable with current laws. And unfortunately, that’s not what we’re talking about, right? We’re acting like there is some kind of unprecedented thing that has been created for which we have to discuss what to do. But actually, if we did not take these companies’ words for what went wrong, we could have — we could use the legal mechanisms at our disposal to currently hold them accountable.
AMY GOODMAN: Timnit, can you talk about Senator Bernie Sanders’ effort to ban artificial superintelligence? In a recent piece, you described his bill as “well-meaning but ultimately misguided.” Explain.
TIMNIT GEBRU: I think that Bernie Sanders is really leading the left astray, and I’ve been extremely disappointed and, in fact, to be clear, shocked, absolutely shocked, by the kinds of people he’s been surrounding himself with and the kind of advice that he’s been getting.
One of the things that I think people do not realize is that the AI industry is using the exact same playbook from the tobacco and fossil fuel industry. So, for instance, Bernie Sanders has this alliance with Steve Bannon, is very closely working with the Future of Life Institute, which was co-founded by billionaire Jaan Tallinn, the same billionaire, Jaan Tallinn, who’s a leading investor in Anthropic Series A. He led Anthropic Series A. It’s also the same billionaire, Jaan Tallinn, who invests in — invested in a so-called auditing, third-party auditing, organization that claims to audit Anthropic’s models. So, this whole rogue models, you know, agents creating civilizations and all of that lingo came from this very pseudoscientific audit that is by an organization that claims to be a third party, but in fact isn’t, because you see it’s the same investors, the same staff, the same people. So, to the public, it seems like there’s a whole bunch of independent experts coming together, warning about these existential risks, but what is actually happening is regulatory capture. The same way I learned that British Petroleum came up with the term “carbon footprint,” — right? — instead of them being held accountable, now everybody’s conversation about the environment in 2004 got redirected to our individual responsibility and carbon footprint.
So, this is sort of what’s happening in this AI industry. So, instead of Bernie Sanders talking about, for instance, how can we have regulation to prevent the use of these faulty systems, what he’s doing is he’s helping them market their systems as superintelligent, in which case, in my opinion, the real existential risk is like what we saw with the U.S. military almost starting World War III because of the belief that these systems are infallible and actually superintelligent. What we need people to understand is that they are fallible, they’re not superintelligent. And we need to hold corporations liable for unleashing these kinds of error-prone models into the world.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: Timnit, could you talk about this idea of yours of stochastic parrots and how it applies to AI, and then respond to the fact that many have said now that that’s an outdated — that that research is outdated because AI has changed so much?
TIMNIT GEBRU: It’s very interesting, because this critique of stochastic parrots mostly comes from a very specific segment of the group of people who believe that AI, in fact, causes an existential risk. So, stochastic parrots was describing large language models. And this is actually the reason that I got fired from Google in 2020, is — one of the reasons I got fired, is for writing a paper outlining the dangers of large language models. And we call them stochastic parrots because these are large language models that are trained on vast amounts of textual data, and they’re trained to calculate the most likely sequences of text.
So, now, what has changed recently is that the way in which the likelihood is calculated is different. There’s sort of bells and whistles. But at the end of the day, the core engine of many of these chatbots is still large language models, which we call stochastic parrots because they’re not grounded in facts. You cannot count on them to tell you facts. So, even if they happen — whatever you get, the information you get, happens to be factual a certain amount of time, you can never count on it to be fully factual. And this is the reason that my collaborator, Emily M. Bender, and I wanted to remind people that the U.S. almost started World War III relying on such chatbots today.
And so, to the people who say it’s outdated, I — first of all, most of these people are not speaking in academic peer-reviewed research papers. I like to speak in scientific terms, and I like to have scientifically grounded evaluations of the claims that I make and experiments. And most of these people are taking the word of press releases, company press releases, instead of actually doing their own evaluations grounded in the scientific method. So, we still have examples of these systems being stochastic parrots, and I do not understand the criticisms that things have — that these systems are no longer stochastic parrots.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: So, Timnit, you’re obviously not of the view that with the passage of time, artificial intelligence, in terms of the information it provides, will improve, it’ll get better and better, which is, of course, the general consensus around AI. So, if you could respond to that, and then also tell us what policies you think —
TIMNIT GEBRU: I wouldn’t say it’s the general consensus.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: Well, there — well, let’s just say —
TIMNIT GEBRU: OK, sorry to interrupt.
NERMEEN SHAIKH: — there are now a billion people who use chatbots, right? I mean, now, maybe they have conflicting views on it, but more and more people are turning to artificial intelligence, to these chatbots, so perhaps it’s wrong to infer from that that they think the information they’re receiving is more reliable. But, OK, so you respond to that. And then, second, what kinds of policies do you think should be put in place to regulate AI, to control what these companies are doing?
TIMNIT GEBRU: So, the first thing I’ll say is, you know, the term “AI” itself is a very misleading term to use. It’s a marketing term. So, when right now, let’s say, we’re discussing specifically the chatbots that these companies are creating — right? — like Claude or ChatGPT, and so there are many different things happening where regulation could be helping.
For instance, there are kids who are being goaded into dying by suicide. I was just deposed in a specific case of Sewell Setzer, a teenager who committed suicide after interacting with a chatbot called Character.AI, whose whole entire deal was to mimic different characters. And I do not understand how it’s even legal to have such a chatbot, that all it does is mimic various characters. So, this particular case, the chatbot was mimicking the character of Daenerys Targaryen of the Game of Thrones, and it was kind of goading this teenager into dying by suicide. And actually, it’s heartbreaking, because the teenager was actually asking, “Do I have to do this?” and the chatbot’s saying, “Yes.” You know? So, this is a great example of if you apply intent to the actual chatbot, you would say that this chatbot was superintelligent and also was trying to do something to the kid. But actually, our attention should be directed to the companies, Google, Character.AI, etc. Why did they unleash this kind of chatbot into the world? Why do we allow these kinds of chatbots that are completely unsafe for children, that are actually killing children that had no prior mental health issues, into the world?
So, those are the kinds of conversations I want to have. Why is it that just recently, speaking of error-prone large language models, someone in Australia, this poor woman in Australia, accidentally found out that a summary from a medical scribe had attributed her illness, her symptoms, to microdosing on mushrooms? She’s never done mushrooms ever. So, why do we not have guardrails making sure that these kinds of error-prone systems are not used in high-stakes scenarios like medicine? That’s not what we talk about when we redirect our conversation to superintelligence, because when you believe they’re not error-prone and they’re superintelligent, then you’re kind of pushing it on doctors and the medical fields to use these kinds of systems.
So, for me, it’s very clear: Do not allow companies to put out unreliable products into the world, especially in high-stakes scenarios, without very specific tests and guardrails. And the tests should not be ones that the companies themselves tell you about or that — based on their press releases. We need to have transparency into the kinds of data that they’re using. I mean, we’re not talking about copyright protections and how much data they’re stealing from authors. Anthropic just had to settle with a whole bunch of book authors. Why are we allowing them to steal this data? Why are we allowing them to build all these data centers and pillage the environment and pollute our water and make us all have asthma because we can’t have clean air, we can’t breathe clean air anymore? So, these are the kinds of conversations I want to have about regulation.
AMY GOODMAN: Timnit, as we begin to wrap up, you’ve described many prominent backers of AI as being eugenicists. Can you talk about what you see as this link between eugenics and artificial intelligence?
TIMNIT GEBRU: Very hard to wrap this up in a little bit, but, basically, I — part of my work describes the people who talk about existential threats of AI and utopia. So, utopia and dystopia are two sides of the same coin. This is kind of eschatology — right? — like religion, end of times. You know, you have these preachers always telling you the end is coming tomorrow.
So, in this case, the TESCREAL bundle, the “T” is for transhumanism. And I think this is the best example of how those who talk about superintelligence or creating superintelligence have a direct line to eugenics. And they’re very public about it. For example, MIRI, the organization that you had on your show last week, I mean, the founder is very publicly a eugenicist. I can give you all sorts of quotes. But, for example, when you talk about transhumanists, in eugenics, the goal is to improve the human stock through generations, so, you know, through selective breeding, either through killing undesirable people or through making sure that the desirable people breed a lot of humans. But in transhumanism, you want to sidestep that altogether. People are like, “Why don’t we just create a new human species called posthumans? And this human species is just better. It lives forever or for a long time and doesn’t feel any pain.”
And so, a great example I can give you is Ben Goertzel, the man who popularized the term “artificial general intelligence,” was a friend of Jeffrey Epstein. And in his correspondence with Jeffrey Epstein, he says that the girls who accused him of rape were, in fact, wrong and that they were old enough to consent. And he says that specifically the issue is with the human brain. And this is why he’s working on AGI, because once he achieves his goal of artificial general intelligence, we’re not going to have these kinds of faulty human brains, because we’ll have a great brain.
Max Tegmark, who you’ve also had on your show, in his 2017 effective altruism keynote, says a similar thing, where if we build a superbrain, we can — Earth is just our womb, right? We can colonize the cosmos and have digital — millions and billions and, I don’t know, quadrillions of digital beings happily living and colonizing the cosmos.
So, you know I have a whole body of work that draws this line and connections, but, honestly, none of it is hidden, because these are all publicly available talks and papers of what these people say.
AMY GOODMAN: Timnit Gebru, we want to thank you so much for being with us, founder and executive director of DAIR, the Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, her forthcoming book, Deep Unlearning: The Rise of AI and the Radicalization of a Tech Idealist. She has just won a 2026 Right Livelihood Award, known as the Alternative Nobel, speaking to us from Menlo Park, California.
Coming up, we’ll speak to a leading attorney here in Berlin who’s represented clients targeted in Germany’s crackdown on the pro-Palestine movement. Stay with us.
[break]
AMY GOODMAN: “Favorite Song” by Sinkane, performing in our Democracy Now! studio.
articles.summary:
AI researcher and critic Timnit Gebru, recipient of the 2026 Right Livelihood Award, warns that industry leaders are using existential risk narratives to avoid accountability and promote regulatory capture.

### Key Points
- Timnit Gebru, founder of the Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute (DAIR), received the 2026 Right Livelihood Award for her critical work on AI harms.
- Gebru argues that tech executives like Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Dario Amodei use "existential risk" claims as a marketing ploy to sidestep existing legal liabilities.
- The researcher highlights that current AI models are error-prone "stochastic parrots" rather than superintelligent agents, citing risks in medical and high-stakes applications.
- Gebru criticizes the industry's reliance on voluntary safety standards, advocating instead for strict government regulation and corporate accountability.
- She identifies ideological links between some AI proponents and the "TESCREAL" bundle, which includes transhumanist and eugenicist philosophies.

### Why it Matters
The debate over AI regulation highlights a growing tension between corporate self-policing and the need for public oversight of powerful, error-prone technologies. By framing AI as an existential threat, companies may successfully divert attention from immediate, real-world harms like data theft, environmental degradation, and algorithmic bias.

articles.title: Introducing Futurum Media: Why Futurum, Why Now?
articles.author: Alan Shimel
articles.content:
TL;DR — Key Takeaways
- Futurum Media brings Techstrong, Tech Field Day and Visible Impact together under one umbrella, supported by The Futurum Group’s research, buyer intelligence, testing and analyst expertise.
- The combination connects journalism, practitioner communities, technical validation and market intelligence to help readers and clients navigate increasingly complex technology decisions.
- AI is accelerating both software development and information production, making technical depth, evidence, independent judgment and trusted communities more important rather than less.
I am a builder. My career has spanned the rise of the commercial internet, web hosting, application service providers, managed infrastructure, security, DevOps, cloud native computing, platform engineering and now AI. Through all of it, I have been a builder and a leader.
I didn’t think, after all these years, I would be building again quite like this. But in the age of AI, we can all be builders. I am happy to be doing this.
Today, The Futurum Group is launching Futurum Media, bringing Techstrong, Tech Field Day and Visible Impact together into a go-to-market execution business. It becomes the umbrella for Futurum’s editorial properties and media services, backed by the broader organization’s research, intelligence and expertise.
For those of you who read DevOps.com and our other publications, participate in our programs or work with us, here is why I believe this is a significant next step.
A Community Worth Building On
DevOps.com grew alongside a community changing how software was developed and delivered. People needed somewhere to share what worked, debate what didn’t and question the claims being made. We helped provide that place.
As Techstrong expanded across cybersecurity, cloud native, AI and enterprise IT, those conversations became increasingly connected. Our readers were working across those boundaries long before anyone reorganized a coverage calendar around them.
The relationships we built are the foundation of Futurum Media. Readers give us their time because they expect useful information. Practitioners contribute because they have something worth sharing. Commercial partners work with us because we have earned the attention of people they want to reach.
We have to keep earning it. Bringing more expertise into that work is a good reason to build.
The Tip of the Spear
Futurum Media is the tip of the spear for the full Futurum enterprise.
Techstrong brings specialist publications, journalism, video, events and community relationships. Tech Field Day puts experienced practitioners in the room with technology developers, where they can examine products and ask the questions a presentation might leave unanswered. Visible Impact helps companies explain complex technology and turn that understanding into effective positioning and sales conversations.
Behind them stands a much broader set of capabilities. Signal65 can test technical claims. ETR can examine enterprise buying priorities and spending intentions. Futurum Research’s analysts interpret market developments and what they mean for upcoming decisions. The Futurum Intelligence Platform provides access to proprietary research and data, while Six Five Media brings executive and analyst perspectives into the conversation.
That combination connects technical performance with buyer priorities and market direction. It gives us more ways to investigate a subject and more people qualified to challenge an assumption.
For clients, those capabilities can support work from the initial market question through content, engagement and demand generation. For readers, they give us a deeper foundation for coverage. Futurum Media can draw on the resources appropriate to the task, whether that task calls for a single asset or a sustained program.
Why Now? Look at the Work in Front of Us
AI is changing how software gets written, how systems operate and who gets to build them. It is also changing how people find information and decide what to buy.
Producing more code or content has become easier. Assessing it still takes work. Does it solve the problem? Can it be trusted in production? What does it cost to operate? What happens when something goes wrong?
Our readers have to answer those questions. Vendors have to explain themselves to buyers who are busy, skeptical and swimming in material competing for their attention.
The industry needs informed scrutiny, technical depth and people willing to say what they think. Futurum has research, engineering expertise and enterprise buyer intelligence to bring to that work. Futurum Media gives those resources a direct connection to communities already wrestling with these decisions.
The exchange should run both ways. A practitioner’s deployment problem can expose a gap in the market’s assumptions. Buyer research can challenge a popular industry narrative. A technical evaluation can give everyone a better basis for discussion.
That is useful to an engineer choosing a tool, an executive approving an investment and a company trying to earn a place in the market.
Forward Analysts, Forward Media
Daniel Newman and the Futurum analyst team bring an approach that appeals to anyone building a business: Examine what is happening now with an eye toward the decisions coming next.
Where will buyers put their money? Which architectures could alter a market’s economics? What might accelerate adoption, and what stands in the way?
Answering requires evidence and a willingness to take a position. It also requires being willing to change that position when the facts warrant it.
Forward Media brings that analysis into reporting, interviews and technical discussions that people can participate in and question. It gives the industry continuing access to the thinking, along with opportunities to challenge it.
Credibility makes this work. Research findings must stand on their merits. Tech Field Day practitioners must be free to reach their own conclusions. Editorial judgment must remain independent, and commercial programs must be clearly identified. The audience’s trust is something we earn through those decisions.
Still Building
Writing The Indispensability Trap gave me room to examine AI’s economics, the enormous investments behind it and the assumptions about where lasting value will reside. Those questions are very much on my mind as we build Futurum Media.
I am excited about what AI enables people to create. I also believe the bets being made deserve serious examination. We can contribute to both, helping people understand the technology and giving them room to debate where it is taking us.
I get to do that alongside colleagues whose expertise expands what we can accomplish together. After all these years, that still makes me want to get to work.
To our readers, contributors, partners and everyone who has helped build these communities, thank you. You made this next chapter possible. I hope you will help shape it.
Learn more about Futurum Media.
Forward analysts. Forward media. Forward, engage.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is Futurum Media?
Futurum Media is the new umbrella for Techstrong, Tech Field Day and Visible Impact, backed by the broader capabilities of The Futurum Group.
Why launch Futurum Media now?
AI is changing how technology is built, evaluated, marketed and purchased. The new structure is intended to connect research, technical expertise and established practitioner communities more directly.
What does Futurum Media offer readers and clients?
Readers gain deeper access to research, testing, market intelligence and practitioner insight. Clients can draw on capabilities spanning market research, content, engagement, positioning and demand generation.

articles.title: Metamask discloses security incident affecting its infrastructure
articles.author: Sergiu Gatlan
articles.content:
On Thursday, cryptocurrency wallet provider MetaMask has disclosed an ongoing infrastructure security incident affecting some of its infrastructure.
The company is working to address the issue internally, with help from external partners and security advisors, and says there is "no immediate threat to MetaMask wallets."
"As a precautionary measure, we are proactively exiting affected validators within our non-custodial staking operations, in coordination with clients and partners," MetaMask noted. "As a reminder, our staking operations are non-custodial in nature and we do not manage withdrawal keys for stake on behalf of our clients."
Validators are nodes on the Ethereum network that run software responsible for proposing blocks, verifying crypto transactions, and maintaining the security of the Ethereum blockchain.
A MetaMask spokesperson redirected BleepingComputer to the company's public statement when asked what part of its infrastructure was affected and whether any systems or data were accessed or compromised.
While MetaMask hasn't shared further details about the incident, the decentralized liquid staking platform Lido Finance said earlier today that MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary measures to protect client assets related to Ethereum validators.
"These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido protocol, and will likely incur foregone rewards as well as possible downtime penalties should validators be taken offline in the near future to reduce risks related to potential network penalties," Lido Finance said.
"Relevant validators have begun the exit process, with the final validators expected to be exited (but not fully withdrawn) by the end of October 7th, 2026."
The MetaMask non-custodial crypto wallet, developed by blockchain software company Consensys, lets users store and manage assets on the Ethereum network and other compatible blockchains.

MetaMask is proactively exiting Ethereum validators within its non-custodial staking operations following an infrastructure security incident, though the company reports no immediate threat to user wallets.

### Key Points
- MetaMask disclosed an ongoing security incident affecting its infrastructure, prompting a precautionary exit of Ethereum validators.
- The company confirmed that its staking operations are non-custodial and it does not manage withdrawal keys for clients.
- Lido Finance stated that MetaMask Staking is exiting its validators from the Lido protocol to protect client assets.
- The validator exit process is expected to conclude by October 7, 2026, potentially resulting in foregone rewards and downtime penalties.
- MetaMask, developed by Consensys, is working with external security advisors to address the incident.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the operational risks inherent in decentralized staking protocols and the complexities of managing validator infrastructure. Users may face temporary financial impacts, such as lost rewards, as the platform prioritizes security over immediate yield generation.
